RollingHMM.name: RollingHMM
RollingHMM.title: Rolling two-state hidden Markov model
RollingHMM.short: Two-state hidden Markov model of a series, refit on a trailing window and filtered forward each step; the probability of the high-variance (or more persistent) state and a one-step predictive mean and standard deviation.

parameters.name: window_size
parameters.description: Number of most recent values the model is fit on.

parameters.name: refit_every
parameters.description: Steps between fits. Between fits the model filters each new value with fixed parameters.

parameters.name: emission
parameters.description: "gaussian": each state emits a normal value with its own mean and variance; "ar1": each state emits an AR(1) step x_t = c + phi x_{t-1} + e with its own c, phi, and variance (Hamilton's Markov-switching AR(1)).

parameters.name: max_iter
parameters.description: Largest number of EM iterations per fit.

parameters.name: tol
parameters.description: A fit stops when an EM iteration raises the log-likelihood by less than this.

references: Hamilton, J. D. (1989). A new approach to the economic analysis of nonstationary time series and the business cycle. *Econometrica* 57(2), 357-384.
Rabiner, L. R. (1989). A tutorial on hidden Markov models and selected applications in speech recognition. *Proceedings of the IEEE* 77(2), 257-286.
RollingHMM.details:
## Description

`RollingHMM` is a two-state hidden Markov model of a series, normally
returns. The series is in one of two states, which persist and switch with
the probabilities of a 2 x 2 transition matrix, and each state emits values
from its own distribution:

- `emission="gaussian"`: state `k` emits `N(mu_k, sigma_k^2)`, for example a
  calm and a volatile regime of returns;
- `emission="ar1"`: state `k` emits `x_t = c_k + phi_k x_{t-1} + sigma_k e_t`,
  Hamilton's (1989) Markov-switching AR(1), for example a trending and a
  reverting regime.

The model is fit by Baum-Welch EM on the last `window_size` values, first on
the step the window fills and then every `refit_every` steps, each fit
starting from the previous one. Between fits each new value updates the state
probability with the fitted parameters (the forward filter). After each fit
the states are ordered so that state 1 is the high-variance state
(`"gaussian"`) or the state with the larger `phi` (`"ar1"`), so the
meaning of the output does not change between fits. Each output at `t` uses
values up to `t`.

It returns three columns:

0. `prob`: the filtered probability of state 1 at `t`.
1. `pred_mean`: the mean of the one-step-ahead predictive distribution, a
   mixture of the two states weighted by their probability at `t + 1`.
2. `pred_std`: the standard deviation of that mixture.

The first `window_size - 1` rows are `NaN`. The first fit starts from a
deterministic split (values below and above the median absolute value for
`"gaussian"`; `phi` at the window's lag-1 autocorrelation minus and plus 0.5
for `"ar1"`), so the result is reproducible. Variances are floored at
`1e-6` times the window variance, which keeps a fit finite on a constant
window. A fit costs `O(max_iter * window_size)`; a step between fits is
`O(1)`.

<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_START -->
## NaN handling

**Policy: `ignore`.** A `NaN` in any input gives a `NaN` output at that step. The step is skipped: it does not enter the window or update the internal state. See [NaN and warmup](../nan_and_warmup.md).
<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_END -->

examples.caption: Usage plot
examples.code:
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots
from screamer import RollingHMM

rng = np.random.default_rng(8)
T = 3000
state = np.zeros(T, dtype=int)
for t in range(1, T):
    stay = 0.99 if state[t - 1] == 0 else 0.98
    state[t] = state[t - 1] if rng.random() < stay else 1 - state[t - 1]
r = rng.standard_normal(T) * np.where(state == 1, 2.0, 0.5)
out = RollingHMM(window_size=1000, refit_every=100)(r)

fig = make_subplots(rows=2, cols=1, shared_xaxes=True, vertical_spacing=0.06)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(y=r, name='returns', line=dict(color='lightgray')), row=1, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(y=out[:, 0], name='P(volatile state)', line=dict(color='crimson')), row=2, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(y=state, name='true state', line=dict(color='gray', dash='dot')), row=2, col=1)
fig.update_layout(title='RollingHMM: the filtered probability of the volatile regime',
                  xaxis2_title='step', margin=dict(l=20, r=20, t=60, b=20),
                  legend=dict(orientation='h', yanchor='bottom', y=1.02, xanchor='right', x=1))
fig.show()

RollingHurst.name: RollingHurst
RollingHurst.title: Rolling Hurst Exponent
RollingHurst.short: Rolling-window Hurst exponent via Anis-Lloyd corrected rescaled-range analysis.

parameters.name: window_size
parameters.description: Trailing-window length W in samples. Must be at least 4 * min_scale so the regression has at least three scales.

parameters.name: min_scale
parameters.description: Smallest R/S block size; the scales are min_scale, 2*min_scale, ... up to window_size/2. Larger values reduce small-sample bias but leave fewer scales for the regression.

parameters.name: method
parameters.description: Estimator family. Only "rs" (Anis-Lloyd corrected rescaled range) is available.

references: Hurst, H. E. (1951). Long-term storage capacity of reservoirs. *Transactions of the American Society of Civil Engineers*, 116, 770-799.
Anis, A. A. and Lloyd, E. H. (1976). The expected value of the adjusted rescaled Hurst range of independent normal summands. *Biometrika*, 63(1), 111-116. doi:10.1093/biomet/63.1.111
Peters, E. E. (1994). *Fractal Market Analysis: Applying Chaos Theory to Investment and Economics*. Wiley.
Weron, R. (2002). Estimating long-range dependence: finite sample properties and confidence intervals. *Physica A*, 312(1-2), 285-299. doi:10.1016/S0378-4371(02)00961-5
Estimating the Hurst exponent. arXiv:1805.08931.
RollingHurst.details:
## Description

`RollingHurst` estimates the Hurst exponent $H$ over a trailing window. $H$ measures
long-range dependence in a time series:

- $H \approx 0.5$: uncorrelated (for example white noise, or the log-returns of a
  geometric Brownian motion).
- $H > 0.5$: persistent (moves tend to continue).
- $H < 0.5$: anti-persistent (moves tend to reverse).

The estimate uses rescaled-range (R/S) analysis with the Anis-Lloyd small-sample
correction. The trailing window of `window_size` samples is split into
non-overlapping blocks of length
$n_k = \texttt{min\_scale}, 2\cdot\texttt{min\_scale}, \dots, W/2$ (dyadic scales).
For each scale the average rescaled range across blocks is corrected for small-sample
bias, and $\hat H$ is the slope of its logarithm against $\log n$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{R/S}(n) &= \frac{1}{\lfloor W/n \rfloor}
  \sum_{p=0}^{\lfloor W/n \rfloor-1}
  \frac{\max_j Y_{p,j} - \min_j Y_{p,j}}{\sigma_p},
  \quad Y_{p,j} = \sum_{i=1}^{j}(x_{p,i} - \bar x_p) \\[2pt]
\text{rsal}(n) &= \text{R/S}(n) - \text{ers}(n) + \sqrt{\tfrac{\pi n}{2}} \\[2pt]
\hat H &= \text{slope of } \log \text{rsal}(n_k) \text{ on } \log n_k
\end{aligned}
$$

where $\text{ers}(n)$ is the Anis-Lloyd expected R/S for $H = 1/2$:

$$
\text{ers}(n) = \frac{\Gamma\!\left(\tfrac{n-1}{2}\right)}{\sqrt{\pi}\,\Gamma\!\left(\tfrac{n}{2}\right)}
\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} \sqrt{\tfrac{n-i}{i}} \qquad (n \le 340; \text{asymptotic form otherwise}).
$$

The first valid output is at sample index `window_size - 1`. The output is also NaN
when any block in the window has zero variance.

## Notes on usage

- For asset prices, apply `RollingHurst` to returns (or log-returns), not to the price
  itself. Prices are close to a random walk, so the estimate on prices is near
  $H \approx 1$ whatever the memory in the returns.
- With `window_size=256` and `min_scale=4` the regression has 6 scales
  (4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128). Smaller windows give noisier estimates; larger windows
  respond more slowly.

<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_START -->
## NaN handling

**Policy: `ignore`.** A `NaN` in any input gives a `NaN` output at that step. The step is skipped: it does not enter the window or update the internal state. See [NaN and warmup](../nan_and_warmup.md).
<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_END -->

examples.caption: Usage example
examples.code:
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from screamer import RollingHurst

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 1500

# Stitch three regimes: white noise, trend (persistent), oscillating (anti-persistent).
wn   = rng.normal(0, 1, n // 3)
drift = 0.05 * np.arange(n // 3) + rng.normal(0, 1, n // 3)
osc  = rng.normal(0, 1, n - 2 * (n // 3))
osc[1::2] *= -1  # zig-zag → strong mean reversion
x = np.concatenate([wn, drift, osc])

H = RollingHurst(window_size=512)(x)

fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(y=x, mode='lines', name='signal',
                         line=dict(color='lightsteelblue'), yaxis='y1'))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(y=H, mode='lines', name='RollingHurst(W=512)',
                         line=dict(color='crimson'), yaxis='y2'))
fig.add_hline(y=0.5, line_dash="dot", line_color="gray",
              annotation_text="H = 0.5 (uncorrelated)", yref='y2')
fig.update_layout(
    title="Hurst exponent across regime changes",
    xaxis_title="Index",
    yaxis=dict(title="signal", side='left'),
    yaxis2=dict(title="Hurst H", side='right', overlaying='y', range=[0, 1]),
    margin=dict(l=20, r=20, t=60, b=20),
    legend=dict(orientation="h", yanchor="bottom", y=1.02, xanchor="right", x=1),
)
fig.show()

RollingIqr.details:
## Description

`RollingIqr` computes the rolling interquartile range:

$$
\text{IQR}[t] = Q_{0.75}[t] - Q_{0.25}[t]
$$

It is a robust spread measure: it ignores the top and bottom quarter of the window, so
a single outlier does not change it. Use it as the denominator of a robust z-score or
as an outlier-resistant volatility measure.

RollingJumpShare.name: RollingJumpShare
RollingJumpShare.title: Rolling Jump Share
RollingJumpShare.short: Share of the realized variance of a window of returns that comes from jumps: max(0, 1 - BV / RV).

parameters.name: window_size
parameters.description: Number of most recent returns in the window.

parameters.name: start_policy
parameters.description: Output before the window is full: "strict" gives NaN, "expanding" uses the returns seen so far (at least two), and "zero" treats the window as pre-filled with zeros.

references: Barndorff-Nielsen, O. E. and Shephard, N. (2004). Power and bipower variation with stochastic volatility and jumps. *Journal of Financial Econometrics* 2(1), 1-37.
RollingJumpShare.details:
## Description

`RollingJumpShare` is `max(0, 1 - BV / RV)`, with `BV` the bipower variation of [`RollingBipowerVar`](RollingBipowerVar.md) and `RV = sum r_i^2` the realized variance of the same window. It is the share of the window's variance that comes from jumps (Barndorff-Nielsen and Shephard 2004): near 0 for diffusive returns and near 1 when a few returns carry most of the variance. On a window of returns `[1, 1, 1, 10]`, `BV = 8 pi`, `RV = 103`, and the share is `0.756`. It is 0 when `RV` is 0, and 0 when `BV` exceeds `RV`, which sampling noise causes on windows without jumps. The result is clamped to the interval 0 to 1.

<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_START -->
## NaN handling

**Policy: `ignore`.** A `NaN` in any input gives a `NaN` output at that step. The step is skipped: it does not enter the window or update the internal state. See [NaN and warmup](../nan_and_warmup.md).
<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_END -->

RollingKurt.title: Rolling kurtosis

parameters.name: window_size
parameters.description: Number of most recent samples in the window. The estimator needs at least 4 samples, so smaller windows give NaN.

parameters.name: start_policy

RollingKurt.details:
## Description

`RollingKurt` computes the excess kurtosis of the `window_size` most recent values,
using the bias-corrected Fisher-Pearson estimator (the same formula as
`pandas.Series.rolling(w).kurt()`). A normal distribution has excess kurtosis zero;
positive values indicate heavier tails. The estimator needs at least 4 samples, so the
output is NaN until 4 samples are in the window.

<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_START -->
## NaN handling

**Policy: `ignore`.** A `NaN` in any input gives a `NaN` output at that step. The step is skipped: it does not enter the window or update the internal state. See [NaN and warmup](../nan_and_warmup.md).

RollingMad.details:
## Description

`RollingMad` computes the rolling mean absolute deviation from the rolling mean:

$$
\text{MAD}[t] = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i \in \text{window}} \left| x_i - \bar{x}_t \right|
$$

It is less sensitive to outliers than [`RollingStd`](RollingStd.md) because it uses
the absolute deviation rather than the squared deviation. It is used in statistical
screening, as the denominator of a robust z-score, and as the scale in [`CCI`](CCI.md). For
the median absolute deviation from the median, use
[`RollingMedianAD`](RollingMedianAD.md).

<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_START -->
## NaN handling

**Policy: `ignore`.** A `NaN` in any input gives a `NaN` output at that step. The step is skipped: it does not enter the window or update the internal state. See [NaN and warmup](../nan_and_warmup.md).
<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_END -->

from screamer import RollingMad

RollingMedianAD.details:
## Description

`RollingMedianAD` computes the rolling **median absolute deviation** (MAD): for the
trailing window it takes the median of the absolute deviations from the window
median,

$$ \text{MAD}_t = \text{median}_{i \in W_t}\; \bigl| x_i - \text{median}(W_t) \bigr|. $$

Unlike [`RollingMad`](RollingMad.md), which is the *mean* absolute deviation, this is
a **robust** scale estimate: a few extreme samples cannot inflate it. It is the scale
primitive behind the [`Hampel`](Hampel.md) and [`ImpulseClip`](ImpulseClip.md)
despikers. The raw MAD is returned; multiply by `1.4826` for a Gaussian-consistent
standard-deviation estimate.

<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_START -->
## NaN handling

**Policy: `ignore`.** A `NaN` in any input gives a `NaN` output at that step. The step is skipped: it does not enter the window or update the internal state. See [NaN and warmup](../nan_and_warmup.md).
<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_END -->

RollingMinMax.details:
## Description

`RollingMinMax` returns the rolling minimum and rolling maximum of a single stream over a sliding window, both computed in one pass.

Use it when you need both extrema together (channels, breakouts, normalized range). Computing them in one pass is roughly half the work of running `RollingMin` and `RollingMax` separately.

*Equation*:

$$
\mathrm{min}_w[t] = \min_{i \in [t-w+1,\, t]} x_i
\qquad
\mathrm{max}_w[t] = \max_{i \in [t-w+1,\, t]} x_i
$$

with the window taking the most recent `window_size` samples.

*Input shape*: a single stream. Same input matrix as the 1-in/1-out functions: scalars, 1-D arrays, 2-D / N-D arrays (axis 0 is time), iterators.

*Output shape*: an extra trailing axis of size **2** is appended to the input shape. A 1-D input of shape `(T,)` returns shape `(T, 2)`; a 2-D input `(T, K)` returns `(T, K, 2)`. Index `0` along the trailing axis is the rolling minimum, index `1` is the rolling maximum.

A scalar call returns a Python `tuple` of two floats.


<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_START -->
## NaN handling

**Policy: `ignore`.** A `NaN` in any input gives a `NaN` output at that step. The step is skipped: it does not enter the window or update the internal state. See [NaN and warmup](../nan_and_warmup.md).
<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_END -->

RollingOU.name: RollingOU
RollingOU.title: Rolling Ornstein-Uhlenbeck fit
RollingOU.short: Rolling MLE fit of a mean-reverting Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process.

parameters.name: window_size
parameters.description: Number of most recent samples in the window.

parameters.name: output
parameters.description: Which fitted parameter to return: "mrr" gives the mean-reversion rate per step, "mean" the long-run mean, "relmean" the long-run mean minus the current value, and "std" the noise standard deviation.

parameters.name: start_policy
parameters.description: Output before the window is full: "strict" gives NaN, "expanding" computes from the samples seen so far, and "zero" treats the window as pre-filled with zeros.

references: Uhlenbeck, G. E. and Ornstein, L. S. (1930). On the theory of the Brownian motion. *Physical Review*, 36(5), 823-841. doi:10.1103/PhysRev.36.823
RollingOU.details:
## Description

`RollingOU` fits a discrete-time Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) model, a mean-reverting process, to the `window_size` most recent values and returns one of the fitted parameters. The fit is refreshed at every step, so the parameters can drift over time.

The discretized form of the OU model is:

$$
x[i] = (1 - \text{mrr}) \cdot x[i-1] + \text{mrr} \cdot \mu + \sigma \cdot \epsilon
$$

where $ x[i] $ is the current value, $ x[i-1] $ is the previous value, $ \mu $ is the mean, $ \text{mrr} $ is the mean reversion rate, $ \sigma $ is the standard deviation of the noise, and $ \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1) $ is a standard normal random variable. The parameter `mrr` controls the rate and nature of mean reversion:

- **0 < mrr < 1**: Values tend to revert to the mean at a rate determined by mrr, with a higher mrr closer to 1 indicating faster mean reversion.
- **mrr < 0**: Values display mean repulsion, where deviations from the mean amplify rather than attenuate.
- **mrr > 1**: Oscillatory behavior or instability arises, as the model overshoots the mean.

The `output` parameter selects $\text{mrr}$, $\mu$ (`"mean"`), $\mu - x[i]$ (`"relmean"`, the distance from the current value to the mean) or $\sigma$ (`"std"`). A larger `window_size` gives smoother estimates that respond more slowly to changes. The half-life of a deviation from the mean, in steps, is $\ln 2 / -\ln(1 - \text{mrr})$ for $0 < \text{mrr} < 1$.

The fit is ordinary least squares of $x[i] = a + b \, x[i-1] + e[i]$ over the $m = $ `window_size` $- 1$ consecutive pairs in the window, with $\text{mrr} = 1 - b$, $\mu = a / (1 - b)$ and $\sigma$ the residual standard deviation with $m - 2$ degrees of freedom. Adding a constant to the input adds it to `"mean"` and leaves the other outputs unchanged, and the pair sums are taken about an origin near the data, so the fit stays accurate on price levels (see [Accuracy at large levels](../conventions.md#accuracy-at-large-levels)). `window_size` must be at least 3, since one pair has no slope. `"std"` needs at least 3 pairs, so it is `NaN` for `window_size=3`, where the residual has no degrees of freedom. With `start_policy="expanding"`, `"mrr"`, `"mean"` and `"relmean"` start at the third value (two pairs) and `"std"` at the fourth.


<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_START -->
## NaN handling

**Policy: `ignore`.** A `NaN` in any input gives a `NaN` output at that step. The step is skipped: it does not enter the window or update the internal state. See [NaN and warmup](../nan_and_warmup.md).
<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_END -->

examples.caption: Usage example
examples.code:
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots
from screamer import RollingOU

# Generate synthetic data with cumulative noise
np.random.seed(0)
data = np.cumsum(np.random.normal(0, 1, 500))

# Define a rolling OU model with window size of 50
rolling_ou_mrr = RollingOU(window_size=50, output="mrr")
rolling_ou_mean = RollingOU(window_size=50, output="mean")
rolling_ou_std = RollingOU(window_size=50, output="std")

# Apply RollingOU on the data for each output type
mrr_estimates = [rolling_ou_mrr(d) for d in data]
mean_estimates = [rolling_ou_mean(d) for d in data]
std_estimates = [rolling_ou_std(d) for d in data]

# Create subplots with original and estimated parameters
fig = make_subplots(rows=4, cols=1, shared_xaxes=True, 
                    row_heights=[1/4, 1/4, 1/4, 1/4], vertical_spacing=0.05)

fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(y=data, mode='lines', name='Original Data'), row=1, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(y=mrr_estimates, mode='lines', name='Mean Reversion Rate (mrr)'), row=2, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(y=mean_estimates, mode='lines', name='Estimated Mean (μ)', line=dict(color='green')), row=3, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(y=std_estimates, mode='lines', name='Noise Std Dev (σ)', line=dict(color='purple')), row=4, col=1)

fig.update_layout(
    title="Rolling Discrete-Time Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Model Parameters",
    xaxis_title="Index",
    yaxis=dict(title="Original Data"),
    yaxis2=dict(title="mrr"),
    yaxis3=dict(title="mean"),
    yaxis4=dict(title="noise"),
    margin=dict(l=20, r=20, t=120, b=20),
    legend=dict(orientation="h", yanchor="bottom", y=1.02, xanchor="right", x=1)        
)

fig.show()

RollingParkinsonVar.short: Var form of the Parkinson range-based volatility estimator (uses high & low).

parameters.name: window_size
parameters.description: Number of most recent bars over which the per-bar estimate is averaged.

references: Parkinson, M. (1980). The extreme value method for estimating the variance of the rate of return. *Journal of Business*, 53(1), 61-65. doi:10.1086/296071
RollingParkinsonVar.details:
## Description

The Parkinson (1980) range-based volatility estimator. Per-bar variance contribution:

$$
\sigma^2_\text{Parkinson}[t] = \frac{1}{4 \ln 2}\ \big(\ln H/L\big)^2
$$

This expression is averaged with a rolling mean over `window_size` bars to form the estimator. `RollingParkinsonVol` returns the square root of `RollingParkinsonVar`.

The inputs are `(high, low)`. Under the model's assumptions (zero drift, no overnight gaps) the estimator is about 5 times as efficient as the close-to-close `RollingStd`.


<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_START -->
## NaN handling

**Policy: `ignore`.** A `NaN` in any input gives a `NaN` output at that step. The step is skipped: it does not enter the window or update the internal state. See [NaN and warmup](../nan_and_warmup.md).
<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_END -->

examples.caption: Usage example
examples.code:
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots
from screamer import RollingParkinsonVar

np.random.seed(0)
close = 100*np.exp(np.cumsum(np.random.normal(0, 0.01, size=300)))
open_ = np.concatenate([[close[0]], close[:-1]])
wick = np.abs(np.random.normal(0, 0.4, size=300))
high = np.maximum(open_, close) + wick
low  = np.minimum(open_, close) - wick
out = RollingParkinsonVar(window_size=20)(high, low)

fig = make_subplots(rows=2, cols=1, shared_xaxes=True,
                    row_heights=[0.55, 0.45], vertical_spacing=0.08)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(y=high, name="high"), row=1, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(y=low, name="low"), row=1, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(y=out, name="RollingParkinsonVar", line=dict(color="red")), row=2, col=1)
fig.update_layout(title="Rolling Parkinson variance (RollingParkinsonVar)",
                  margin=dict(l=20, r=20, t=60, b=20),
                  legend=dict(orientation="h", yanchor="bottom", y=1.02, xanchor="right", x=1))
fig.update_yaxes(title_text="price", row=1, col=1)
fig.update_yaxes(title_text="variance", row=2, col=1)
fig.show()

RollingPermutationEntropy.details:
## Description

`RollingPermutationEntropy` is the permutation entropy of Bandt and Pompe
(2002) over a trailing window. At each step, the `order` values
`x[t - (order-1)*delay], ..., x[t - delay], x[t]` form an ordinal pattern: the
order of their ranks, one of `order!` possibilities. The output is the Shannon
entropy of the patterns that end at the last `window_size` steps, divided by
`log(order!)`:

$$
H = -\frac{1}{\log(\text{order}!)} \sum_{\pi} p_\pi \log p_\pi
$$

where `p_pi` is the share of pattern `pi` in the window. `H` is 0 when one
pattern fills the window, such as on a monotone or constant series, and near 1
when every pattern is equally frequent, as for white noise. Values in between
mean that some orderings are more common than others, which a forecast can
use.

Equal values rank by order of appearance, the earlier one lower, so on prices
that repeat a tick, `(2, 1, 1)` and `(1, 1, 2)` are two patterns. The input can
be prices or returns; a pattern of prices describes the signs of the moves
between them.

<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_START -->
## NaN handling

**Policy: `ignore`.** A `NaN` in any input gives a `NaN` output at that step. The step is skipped: it does not enter the window or update the internal state. See [NaN and warmup](../nan_and_warmup.md).
<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_END -->

                  xaxis_title='step', yaxis_title='normalized entropy',

`RollingPoly1` fits a straight line by least squares to the `window_size` most recent values and returns either the line's value at the newest sample (`derivative_order=0`) or its slope (`derivative_order=1`). RollingRSI.name: RollingRSI
RollingRSI.title: Rolling RSI
RollingRSI.short: Relative Strength Index. Wilder's smoothing by default; Cutler's via method='cutler'.

parameters.name: window_size
parameters.description: Smoothing period of the average up and down moves. Wilder's original choice is 14.

parameters.name: method
parameters.description: Smoothing of the up and down moves: "wilder" uses Wilder's recursive average (matches TA-Lib and pandas-ta), "cutler" uses a simple moving average.

parameters.name: start_policy
parameters.description: Output before the window is full: "strict" gives NaN, "expanding" computes from the samples seen so far, and "zero" treats the window as pre-filled with zeros.

references: Wilder, J. W. (1978). *New Concepts in Technical Trading Systems*. Trend Research.
RollingRSI.details:
## Description

Wilder's Relative Strength Index. Up- and down-moves are separately smoothed; the index
is `100 - 100 / (1 + RS)` where `RS` is the smoothed ratio of average up to average down
moves:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Delta[t] &= x[t] - x[t-1] \\
U[t] &= \max(\Delta, 0),\quad D[t] = \max(-\Delta, 0) \\
\overline{U}[t] &= \text{smooth}(U,\ \text{window\_size}),\quad \overline{D}[t] = \text{smooth}(D,\ \text{window\_size}) \\
\text{RS}[t] &= \overline{U}[t] / \overline{D}[t] \\
\text{RSI}[t] &= 100 - 100 / (1 + \text{RS})
\end{aligned}
$$

The smoothing depends on `method`:

- `'wilder'` (default): Wilder's smoothing
  $\overline{X}[t] = \overline{X}[t-1] + (X[t] - \overline{X}[t-1]) / w$, seeded with
  the simple mean of the first `w` values. Matches `talib.RSI` and `pandas-ta-classic.rsi`
  bit-exactly after warmup.
- `'cutler'`: Cutler's variant, a plain rolling mean of the last `w` values. It does
  not match TA-Lib.

The first valid output is at sample index `window_size`, and the output lies in `[0, 100]`.


<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_START -->
## NaN handling

**Policy: `ignore`.** A `NaN` in any input gives a `NaN` output at that step. The step is skipped: it does not enter the window or update the internal state. See [NaN and warmup](../nan_and_warmup.md).
<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_END -->

RollingRogersSatchellVar.short: Var form of the Rogers-Satchell drift-robust range-based estimator.

parameters.name: window_size
parameters.description: Number of most recent bars over which the per-bar estimate is averaged.

references: Rogers, L. C. G. and Satchell, S. E. (1991). Estimating variance from high, low and closing prices. *Annals of Applied Probability*, 1(4), 504-512. doi:10.1214/aoap/1177005835
RollingRogersSatchellVar.details:
## Description

The Rogers-Satchell (1991) range-based volatility estimator. Per-bar variance contribution:

$$
\sigma^2_\text{RS}[t] = \ln\tfrac{H}{C}\ \ln\tfrac{H}{O} + \ln\tfrac{L}{C}\ \ln\tfrac{L}{O}
$$

This expression is averaged with a rolling mean over `window_size` bars to form the estimator. `RollingRogersSatchellVol` returns the square root of `RollingRogersSatchellVar`.

The inputs are `(open, high, low, close)`. The estimator is about 6 times as efficient as close-to-close, slightly less than Garman-Klass, and unlike Garman-Klass it stays unbiased when the price has a non-zero drift, as in trending markets.


<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_START -->
## NaN handling

**Policy: `ignore`.** A `NaN` in any input gives a `NaN` output at that step. The step is skipped: it does not enter the window or update the internal state. See [NaN and warmup](../nan_and_warmup.md).
<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_END -->

RollingSeasonalMean.short: Mean of the same slot of the last `window_size` cycles, such as the same hour on each of the last 20 days.

parameters.name: period
parameters.description: Steps per cycle, for example 24 for hourly data with a daily cycle.

parameters.name: window_size
parameters.description: Number of cycles in the window.

parameters.name: start_policy
parameters.description: Output before a slot holds window_size values: "strict" gives NaN, "expanding" uses the values the slot holds, and "zero" starts each slot with window_size zeros.

RollingSeasonalMean.details:
## Description

`RollingSeasonalMean` is the mean of one slot of a cycle over the last
`window_size` cycles:

$$
\text{mean}_t = \frac{1}{w} \sum_{j=0}^{w-1} x_{t - j \cdot \text{period}}
$$

Step `t` belongs to slot `t mod period`, counted in steps from the first input,
so the input must be on a regular clock: one value per hour for `period=24`,
for example. On hourly volume the current hour of the day is compared with the
same hour on the last `window_size` days.

A `NaN` step advances the slot clock and enters no window, and its output is
`NaN`: a missing hour is treated as missing, and the hours after it stay in

RollingSeasonalStd.details:
## Description

`RollingSeasonalStd` is the sample standard deviation (ddof 1) of one slot of a
cycle over the last `window_size` cycles:

$$
\text{std}_t = \sqrt{\frac{1}{w-1} \sum_{j=0}^{w-1} \left(x_{t - j \cdot \text{period}} - \text{mean}_t\right)^2}
$$

Step `t` belongs to slot `t mod period`, counted in steps from the first input,
so the input must be on a regular clock: one value per hour for `period=24`,
for example. On hourly volume the current hour of the day is compared with the
same hour on the last `window_size` days.

A `NaN` step advances the slot clock and enters no window, and its output is
`NaN`: a missing hour is treated as missing, and the hours after it stay in
their own slots. With `period=2, window_size=2` and `start_policy="expanding"`,
the input `[1, 10, NaN, 20, 5, 30]` gives `[NaN, NaN, NaN, 7.07, 2.83, 7.07]`, where the `NaN` at index 2 is the missing step.

## Description

`RollingSeasonalZscore` standardizes each value against the same slot of the last
`window_size` cycles:

$$
z_t = \frac{x_t - \text{mean}_t}{\text{std}_t}

that includes `x_t`, as in [`RollingZscore`](RollingZscore.md). With `period=1`
it equals `RollingZscore(window_size)`. On hourly volume it flags an hour that
is unusual for that hour of the day.

Step `t` belongs to slot `t mod period`, counted in steps from the first input,
so the input must be on a regular clock: one value per hour for `period=24`,
for example. On hourly volume the current hour of the day is compared with the
same hour on the last `window_size` days.

A `NaN` step advances the slot clock and enters no window, and its output is
`NaN`: a missing hour is treated as missing, and the hours after it stay in
their own slots. With `period=2, window_size=2` and `start_policy="expanding"`,
the input `[1, 10, NaN, 20, 5, 30]` gives `[NaN, NaN, NaN, 0.71, 0.71, 0.71]`, where the `NaN` at index 2 is the missing step.

RollingSigmaClip.title: Rolling sigma-clip
RollingSigmaClip.short: Clip samples that lie beyond lower or upper standard deviations from the rolling mean, or replace them with NaN.

parameters.name: window_size
parameters.description: Number of most recent samples in the window.

parameters.name: lower
parameters.description: Lower clipping threshold in standard deviations from the rolling mean (for example -3). None disables lower clipping. NaN and -inf also disable it.

parameters.name: upper
parameters.description: Upper clipping threshold in standard deviations from the rolling mean (for example 3). None disables upper clipping. NaN and inf also disable it.

parameters.name: output
parameters.description: Which value to return: "clipped" gives the input with outliers clipped to the bound, "mean" the rolling mean estimate, "std" the rolling standard deviation estimate, and "nan" the input with outliers replaced by NaN.

parameters.name: start_policy
parameters.description: Output before the window is full: "strict" gives NaN, "expanding" computes from the samples seen so far, and "zero" treats the window as pre-filled with zeros.

RollingSigmaClip.details:
## Description

`RollingSigmaClip` clips outliers against a rolling mean and standard deviation. Each new value is compared with the bounds `mean + lower * std` and `mean + upper * std`; a value outside them is replaced by the bound it crossed (or by `NaN` with `output="nan"`). Clipped values are left out of the window, so they do not inflate later estimates. Because the window then holds only values inside the bounds, its mean and standard deviation are corrected for truncation, assuming the data is normally distributed (see Implementation Details).


<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_START -->
## NaN handling

**Policy: `ignore`.** A `NaN` in any input gives a `NaN` output at that step. The step is skipped: it does not enter the window or update the internal state. See [NaN and warmup](../nan_and_warmup.md).
<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_END -->

examples.caption: Usage example
examples.code:
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots
from screamer import RollingSigmaClip

# Generate example data with outliers
np.random.seed(42)
data = np.random.normal(loc=0, scale=1, size=300)
data[::50] += np.random.normal(loc=0, scale=10, size=6)  # Introduce outliers

# Rolling Clipping Settings
window_size = 30
lower_z = -3  # Lower z-score threshold
upper_z = 3   # Upper z-score threshold

# Get the clipped data
clipped_data = RollingSigmaClip(window_size=window_size, lower=lower_z, upper=upper_z)(data)
rolling_mean = RollingSigmaClip(window_size=window_size, lower=lower_z, upper=upper_z, output="mean")(data)
rolling_std = RollingSigmaClip(window_size=window_size, lower=lower_z, upper=upper_z, output="std")(data)

# Calculate upper and lower bounds
upper_bound = rolling_mean + upper_z * rolling_std
lower_bound = rolling_mean + lower_z * rolling_std

# Create subplots
fig = make_subplots(rows=2, cols=1, shared_xaxes=True, vertical_spacing=0.1)

# Plot input data
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(y=data, mode='lines', name='Input Data'), row=1, col=1)

# Plot rolling mean and bounds
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(y=clipped_data, mode='lines', name='Clipped Data', line=dict(color='red')), row=2, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(y=rolling_mean, mode='lines', name='Rolling Mean', line=dict(color='gray', dash='dash')), row=2, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(y=upper_bound, mode='lines', name='Bounds', line=dict(color='orange',  dash='dash')), row=2, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(y=lower_bound, mode='lines', line=dict(color='orange', dash='dash'),showlegend=False), row=2, col=1)

# Update layout
fig.update_layout(
    title=f"Rolling Sigma Clipping, Window Size {window_size}, bounds ({lower_z}, {upper_z})",
    xaxis_title="Index",
    yaxis_title="Value",
    yaxis=dict(title="Data", range=[-5, 5]),
    yaxis2=dict(title="Output", range=[-5, 5]),  
    margin=dict(l=20, r=20, t=80, b=20),
    legend=dict(orientation="h", yanchor="bottom", y=1.02, xanchor="right", x=1)
)

fig.show()

RollingVWAP.details:
## Description

Rolling volume-weighted average price using the typical price as the weighting basis:

$$
\text{TP}[t] = (\text{high} + \text{low} + \text{close}) / 3
\qquad
\text{VWAP}[t] = \dfrac{\sum_w \text{TP} \cdot \text{volume}}{\sum_w \text{volume}}
$$

The inputs are `(high, low, close, volume)`. Matches `pandas-ta-classic.vwap`. For a session VWAP (cumulative since a reset point), call `reset()` at the session boundary.

The first valid output is at sample index `window_size - 1`. The two sums are kept as running window sums, so each step is O(1).


<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_START -->
## NaN handling

**Policy: `ignore`.** A `NaN` in any input gives a `NaN` output at that step. The step is skipped: it does not enter the window or update the internal state. See [NaN and warmup](../nan_and_warmup.md).
<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_END -->

examples.caption: Usage example
examples.code:
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots
from screamer import RollingVWAP

np.random.seed(0)
close = 100*np.exp(np.cumsum(np.random.normal(0, 0.01, size=300)))
open_ = np.concatenate([[close[0]], close[:-1]])
wick = np.abs(np.random.normal(0, 0.4, size=300))
high = np.maximum(open_, close) + wick
low  = np.minimum(open_, close) - wick
volume = np.random.uniform(1e5, 5e5, size=300)
vwap = RollingVWAP(window_size=20)(high, low, close, volume)

fig = make_subplots(rows=2, cols=1, shared_xaxes=True,
                    row_heights=[0.55, 0.45], vertical_spacing=0.08)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(y=close, name="close"), row=1, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(y=vwap, name="RollingVWAP", line=dict(color="red")), row=1, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Bar(y=volume, name="volume"), row=2, col=1)

                  margin=dict(l=20, r=20, t=60, b=20),
                  legend=dict(orientation="h", yanchor="bottom", y=1.02, xanchor="right", x=1))
fig.update_yaxes(title_text="price", row=1, col=1)
fig.update_yaxes(title_text="volume", row=2, col=1)
fig.show()

RollingVarianceRatio.title: Rolling Variance Ratio
RollingVarianceRatio.short: Lo-MacKinlay variance ratio of a window of returns, near 1 for a random walk, above 1 when returns trend and below 1 when they revert, or its robust z-statistic.

parameters.name: window_size
parameters.description: Number of most recent returns in the window. Must be more than 2 lag.

parameters.name: lag
parameters.description: Number of returns summed into each long-horizon return (q).

parameters.name: output
parameters.description: "ratio" for the variance ratio VR(q), "zscore" for the heteroskedasticity-robust statistic z*(q).

parameters.name: start_policy
parameters.description: Output before the window is full: "strict" gives NaN, "expanding" uses the returns seen so far once there are more than 2 lag, and "zero" treats the window as pre-filled with zeros.

references: Lo, A. W. and MacKinlay, A. C. (1988). Stock market prices do not follow random walks: evidence from a simple specification test. *Review of Financial Studies* 1(1), 41-66.
RollingVarianceRatio.details:
## Description

`RollingVarianceRatio` is the variance ratio of Lo and MacKinlay (1988) on a
trailing window of `n` returns: the variance of the overlapping `q`-step sums
of returns, divided by `q` times the variance of one-step returns, with
`q = lag`. Returns that are uncorrelated give a ratio near 1; returns that
continue in the same direction (a trend) give more than 1; returns that
reverse (mean reversion) give less than 1.

With `mu` the window mean, the one-step variance is
`sum (r_i - mu)^2 / (n - 1)` and the `q`-step variance is the sum of the
squared deviations of the `n - q + 1` overlapping `q`-sums from `q mu`,
divided by `m = q (n - q + 1)(1 - q / n)`; both are the authors'
bias-corrected estimators. On the returns `[1, -1, 1, -1, 1]` with `lag=2`,
every 2-sum is 0 and the ratio is `1/9`.

`output="zscore"` gives the heteroskedasticity-robust statistic `z*(q)`, which
is approximately standard normal when the returns are uncorrelated, even with
changing volatility; `|z*| > 1.96` rejects a random walk at the 5% level. The
output is `NaN` on a window whose returns are all equal, and for `"zscore"` also when
no two nonzero deviations from the mean lie within `lag` steps of each other.

<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_START -->
## NaN handling

**Policy: `ignore`.** A `NaN` in any input gives a `NaN` output at that step. The step is skipped: it does not enter the window or update the internal state. See [NaN and warmup](../nan_and_warmup.md).
<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_END -->

import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from screamer import RollingVarianceRatio

rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
e = rng.standard_normal(3000)
r = np.empty(3000)
r[0] = e[0]
for t in range(1, 3000):
    phi = 0.3 if t < 1500 else -0.3         # trending, then reverting
    r[t] = phi * r[t - 1] + e[t]
vr = RollingVarianceRatio(250, lag=5)(r)

fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(y=vr, name='VR(5)', line=dict(color='navy')))
fig.add_hline(y=1.0, line=dict(color='gray', dash='dot'))
fig.update_layout(title='RollingVarianceRatio: above 1 while returns trend, below 1 while they revert',
                  xaxis_title='step', yaxis_title='variance ratio',
                  margin=dict(l=20, r=20, t=60, b=20), showlegend=False)

parameters.description: Number of bars n in each variance component; the first estimate needs n + 1 bars.

references: Yang, D. and Zhang, Q. (2000). Drift-independent volatility estimation based on high, low, open, and close prices. *Journal of Business*, 73(3), 477-491. doi:10.1086/209650
RollingYangZhangVar.details:
## Description

The Yang-Zhang (2000) estimator combines three variance components:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sigma^2_o    &= \text{sample variance of overnight log returns } \ln(O_t / C_{t-1}) \\
\sigma^2_c    &= \text{sample variance of open-to-close log returns } \ln(C_t / O_t) \\
\sigma^2_{RS} &= \text{mean of per-bar Rogers-Satchell estimates} \\
k             &= \dfrac{0.34}{1.34 + (n+1)/(n-1)} \\
\sigma^2_{YZ} &= \sigma^2_o + k\ \cdot\ \sigma^2_c + (1-k)\ \cdot\ \sigma^2_{RS}
\end{aligned}
$$

where `n = window_size`. The estimator is unbiased under both a non-zero drift and overnight gaps, and Yang and Zhang report an efficiency of up to about 14 times close-to-close.

The inputs are `(open, high, low, close)`. The first valid output is at sample index `window_size`, because `n` overnight returns need `n + 1` bars. `RollingYangZhangVol` returns the square root of `RollingYangZhangVar`. The exponentially weighted form, `EwYangZhangVar`, replaces the window size in `k` with an effective sample count derived from the decay.


<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_START -->
## NaN handling

**Policy: `ignore`.** A `NaN` in any input gives a `NaN` output at that step. The step is skipped: it does not enter the window or update the internal state. See [NaN and warmup](../nan_and_warmup.md).
<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_END -->

RollingZscore.short: Latest sample standardized by the trailing-window mean and standard deviation.

parameters.name: window_size
parameters.description: Number of most recent samples in the window.

parameters.name: start_policy
parameters.description: Output before the window is full: "strict" gives NaN, "expanding" computes from the samples seen so far, and "zero" treats the window as pre-filled with zeros.

RollingZscore.details:
## Description

`RollingZscore` standardizes each new value against the trailing window:

$$
z[t] = \frac{x[t] - \bar{x}_w[t]}{\text{std}_w[t]}
$$

where `std` is the sample standard deviation (ddof=1) over the `window_size` most recent values.

Before the window is full, `start_policy` works as for `RollingMean` and `RollingStd`: `"strict"` gives `NaN`, `"expanding"` uses the values seen so far (the first output is `NaN`, since one value has no standard deviation), and `"zero"` counts the missing values as zeros.


<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_START -->
## NaN handling

**Policy: `ignore`.** A `NaN` in any input gives a `NaN` output at that step. The step is skipped: it does not enter the window or update the internal state. See [NaN and warmup](../nan_and_warmup.md).

Stoch.name: Stoch
Stoch.title: Stochastic Oscillator
Stoch.short: Stochastic oscillator %K and %D from high, low and close.

parameters.name: fastk_period
parameters.description: Number of most recent bars over which the highest high and lowest low are taken for raw %K.

parameters.name: smooth_k
parameters.description: Period of the simple moving average applied to raw %K; 1 gives the fast stochastic, 3 the slow stochastic of TA-Lib.

parameters.name: d
parameters.description: Period of the simple moving average applied to %K to produce %D.

references: Lane, G. C. (1984). Lane's stochastics. *Technical Analysis of Stocks & Commodities*, 2(3), 87-90.
Stoch.details:
## Description

`Stoch` (the stochastic oscillator of George Lane) returns the pair `(%K, %D)` per step. The raw stochastic measures where the close sits within the recent high-low range, scaled to `[0, 100]`. Two layers of simple moving average smoothing then give the "fast" and "slow" variants.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{raw\_K}[t] &= 100 \cdot \frac{C - L_n}{H_n - L_n} \\
\%K[t]           &= \text{SMA}(\text{raw\_K},\ \text{smooth\_k}) \\
\%D[t]           &= \text{SMA}(\%K,\ d)
\end{aligned}
$$

The inputs are `(high, low, close)`, and the outputs are `%K` and `%D`.

## Common configurations

The common variants differ only in `smooth_k`:

| Configuration | Constructor | TA-Lib equivalent |
|---|---|---|
| **Slow Stochastic** (charting default; what `talib.STOCH` returns) | `Stoch(14, 3, 3)` | `STOCH(high, low, close, fastk_period=14, slowk_period=3, slowd_period=3)` |
| **Fast Stochastic** (Lane's original, no smoothing of %K) | `Stoch(14, 1, 3)` | `STOCHF(high, low, close, fastk_period=14, fastd_period=3)` |
| TA-Lib's *function* defaults (rarely used by traders) | `Stoch(5, 3, 3)` | `STOCH(..., fastk_period=5, slowk_period=3, slowd_period=3)` |

With `smooth_k=1` the moving average of period 1 is the identity, so `%K = raw_K` and the class returns the fast variant.

## Warmup and edge cases

Both outputs are NaN until the `%D` line is valid, at sample index `fastk_period + smooth_k + d - 3`. This follows TA-Lib, which starts both lines together. For the default `(14, 3, 3)` that is index 17.

When `H_n == L_n` over the period (a flat segment) the raw stochastic is undefined, and `Stoch` returns 0, matching TA-Lib.

## Implementation Details

The rolling high and low are kept in two monotonic deques, and the two smoothing stages are rolling means.

* Time complexity: `O(1)` amortized per step.
* Space complexity: `O(fastk_period + smooth_k + d)`.

## Output shape

`%K` is `out[..., 0]` and `%D` is `out[..., 1]`:

| You pass... | You get back... |
|---|---|
| three scalars | tuple `(%K, %D)` |
| three 1D arrays of shape `(T,)` | array of shape `(T, 2)` |
| three 2D arrays of shape `(T, K)` | array of shape `(T, K, 2)` |


<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_START -->
## NaN handling

**Policy: `ignore`.** A `NaN` in any input gives a `NaN` output at that step. The step is skipped: it does not enter the window or update the internal state. See [NaN and warmup](../nan_and_warmup.md).
<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_END -->

low = close - np.abs(rng.normal(0, 0.5, n))

StochRSI.title: Stochastic RSI
StochRSI.short: Stochastic oscillator applied to the RSI, giving %K and %D.

parameters.name: rsi_period
parameters.description: Smoothing period of the Wilder RSI computed from the input.

parameters.name: stoch_period
parameters.description: Number of most recent RSI values over which the minimum and maximum are taken.

parameters.name: smooth_k
parameters.description: Period of the simple moving average applied to raw %K; 1 gives the fast StochRSI.

parameters.name: d
parameters.description: Period of the simple moving average applied to %K to produce %D.

references: Chande, T. S. and Kroll, S. (1994). *The New Technical Trader*. John Wiley & Sons.
StochRSI.details:
## Description

`StochRSI` (Chande and Kroll, 1994) applies the stochastic oscillator formula to an RSI series rather than to price: it expresses the current RSI value as a position within its own rolling min-max range.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{RSI}[t]   &= \text{RollingRSI}(\text{rsi\_period},\ \text{method}=\text{wilder})(x)[t] \\
\text{raw\_K}   &= 100 \cdot \frac{\text{RSI} - \min(\text{RSI},\ \text{stoch\_period})}{\max(\text{RSI},\ \text{stoch\_period}) - \min(\text{RSI},\ \text{stoch\_period})} \\
\%K[t]          &= \text{SMA}(\text{raw\_K},\ \text{smooth\_k}) \\
\%D[t]          &= \text{SMA}(\%K,\ d)
\end{aligned}
$$

It takes one input and returns two outputs, `%K` and `%D`.

## Common configurations

| Configuration | Constructor | TA-Lib equivalent |
|---|---|---|
| **Fast StochRSI** (TA-Lib's `STOCHRSI`, the default) | `StochRSI(14, 14, 1, 3)` | `STOCHRSI(close, timeperiod=14, fastk_period=14, fastd_period=3)` |
| **Slow StochRSI** (smoothing on %K) | `StochRSI(14, 14, 3, 3)` | not in TA-Lib; common in pandas-ta `stochrsi(..., k=3, ...)` |

With `smooth_k=1` the moving average is the identity, so `%K = raw_K` (the fast form). `smooth_k >= 2` gives the slow form.

## Warmup and edge cases

Both outputs are NaN until `%D` is valid, at sample index `rsi_period + stoch_period + smooth_k + d - 3`. This follows TA-Lib, which starts both lines together. For the defaults that is index 29.

When the RSI window is flat (`max == min`), `raw_K` is undefined and `StochRSI` returns 0.


<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_START -->
## NaN handling

**Policy: `ignore`.** A `NaN` in any input gives a `NaN` output at that step. The step is skipped: it does not enter the window or update the internal state. See [NaN and warmup](../nan_and_warmup.md).
<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_END -->

TEMA.name: TEMA
TEMA.title: Triple Exponential MA (TEMA)

parameters.name: com
parameters.description: Center of mass c, giving alpha = 1 / (1 + c). Must be positive. Give exactly one of com, span, halflife and alpha.

parameters.name: span
parameters.description: Span s in samples, giving alpha = 2 / (s + 1). Must be greater than 1. Give exactly one of com, span, halflife and alpha. The default shown is an example value; the constructor has no default.

parameters.name: halflife
parameters.description: Half-life h in samples, giving alpha = 1 - exp(-ln(2) / h). Must be positive. Give exactly one of com, span, halflife and alpha.

parameters.name: alpha
parameters.description: Smoothing factor, with 0 < alpha < 1; a larger alpha gives recent samples more weight. Give exactly one of com, span, halflife and alpha.

references: Mulloy, P. G. (1994). Smoothing data with less lag. *Technical Analysis of Stocks & Commodities*, 12(2), 72-80.
TEMA.details:
## Description

`TEMA` (triple exponential moving average, Patrick Mulloy, 1994) extends the `DEMA` construction by one more level:

$$
\text{TEMA}[t] = 3 \cdot \text{EMA}(x)[t] - 3 \cdot \text{EMA}(\text{EMA}(x))[t] + \text{EMA}(\text{EMA}(\text{EMA}(x)))[t]
$$

The three-term combination reduces lag further: `TEMA` typically tracks the input faster than `DEMA`, and much faster than a plain EMA of the same span, at the cost of less smoothing. The decay parameter (exactly one of `com`, `span`, `halflife` or `alpha`, as in `EwMean`) is shared by all three EMAs.

## Implementation Details

### Algorithm

`TEMA` chains three `EwMean` stages. It has no warmup: each `EwMean` returns a valid value from t=0, so `TEMA[0] = 3*x[0] - 3*x[0] + x[0] = x[0]`.

### Complexity

* Time complexity: `O(1)` per step.
* Space complexity: `O(1)`.


<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_START -->
## NaN handling

**Policy: `ignore`.** A `NaN` in any input gives a `NaN` output at that step. The step is skipped: it does not enter the window or update the internal state. See [NaN and warmup](../nan_and_warmup.md).
<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_END -->

TRIMA.name: TRIMA
TRIMA.title: Triangular MA (TRIMA)
TRIMA.short: Triangular moving average: a simple moving average of a simple moving average.

parameters.name: window_size
parameters.description: Total width of the triangular weighting, in samples.

TRIMA.details:
## Description

`TRIMA` (triangular moving average) is a simple moving average of a simple moving average. The effective per-sample weights form a symmetric triangle, rising then falling, so the center of the window gets more weight than the ends.

$$
\text{TRIMA}(x, n)[t] = \text{SMA}(\text{SMA}(x, n_\text{inner}), n_\text{outer})[t]
$$

with TA-Lib's window split:

| Total window `n` | `n_inner` | `n_outer` |
|---|---|---|
| odd | `(n + 1) / 2` | `(n + 1) / 2` |
| even | `n/2 + 1` | `n/2` |

In both cases `n_inner + n_outer - 1 == n`, so the effective triangular weighting spans `n` samples.

## Implementation Details

### Algorithm

`TRIMA` chains two rolling means. Both run over partial windows during warmup, so the inner mean never passes `NaN` to the outer one; `TRIMA` itself returns `NaN` until `n` samples have been processed.

### Complexity

* Time complexity: `O(1)` per step (two `RollingMean` updates).
* Space complexity: `O(window_size)`.


<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_START -->
## NaN handling

**Policy: `ignore`.** A `NaN` in any input gives a `NaN` output at that step. The step is skipped: it does not enter the window or update the internal state. See [NaN and warmup](../nan_and_warmup.md).

TRIX.name: TRIX
TRIX.title: TRIX (rate of change of triple EMA)

parameters.name: span
parameters.description: Span of each of the three exponential moving averages, giving alpha = 2 / (span + 1).

references: Hutson, J. K. (1983). Good TRIX. *Technical Analysis of Stocks & Commodities*, 1(5), 105-108.
TRIX.details:
## Description

`TRIX(span)` (Jack Hutson, 1983) is the one-step percentage rate of change of a triple-smoothed EMA. It is a momentum oscillator: the two extra layers of exponential smoothing filter out short-term noise before the change is measured.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{ema}_1[t] &= \text{EwMean}(\text{span})(x)[t] \\
\text{ema}_2[t] &= \text{EwMean}(\text{span})(\text{ema}_1)[t] \\
\text{ema}_3[t] &= \text{EwMean}(\text{span})(\text{ema}_2)[t] \\
\text{TRIX}[t]  &= 100 \cdot \frac{\text{ema}_3[t] - \text{ema}_3[t-1]}{\text{ema}_3[t-1]}
\end{aligned}
$$

All three stages use the same `span`. Only the first output is NaN, because there is no previous `ema3` yet; each `EwMean` is defined from `t=0`, so TRIX is finite from `t=1` onward.

## Implementation Details

`TRIX` chains three `EwMean` stages and keeps the previous `ema3` value. Each step is O(1).

The underlying EMA follows pandas `adjust=True` (the bias-corrected weighted mean used throughout the library). TA-Lib's TRIX uses `adjust=False` with an SMA-seeded warmup, so ours differs from TA-Lib by a few percent during early samples; see [conventions](../conventions.md).


<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_START -->
## NaN handling

**Policy: `ignore`.** A `NaN` in any input gives a `NaN` output at that step. The step is skipped: it does not enter the window or update the internal state. See [NaN and warmup](../nan_and_warmup.md).
<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_END -->

references: Wilder, J. W. (1978). *New Concepts in Technical Trading Systems*. Trend Research.
TrueRange.details:
## Description

`TrueRange` returns Wilder's per-bar true range, the bar's high-low range extended to include a gap from the previous close:

$$
\text{TR}[t] = \max\big(\ H - L,\ \ |H - C_{t-1}|,\ \ |L - C_{t-1}|\ \big)
$$

The inputs are `(high, low, close)`. The first output is `NaN` because there is no previous close; after that, each output depends only on the current bar and the previous close. Bit-exact to `talib.TRANGE`.


<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_START -->
## NaN handling

**Policy: `ignore`.** A `NaN` in any input gives a `NaN` output at that step. The step is skipped: it does not enter the window or update the internal state. See [NaN and warmup](../nan_and_warmup.md).
<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_END -->

UltimateOscillator.name: UltimateOscillator
UltimateOscillator.title: Ultimate Oscillator

parameters.name: period1
parameters.description: Shortest of the three averaging periods, in bars; weighted 4.

parameters.name: period2
parameters.description: Middle averaging period, in bars; weighted 2.

parameters.name: period3
parameters.description: Longest averaging period, in bars; weighted 1. Output starts once this window is full.

references: Williams, L. (1985). The ultimate oscillator. *Technical Analysis of Stocks & Commodities*, 3(4), 140-141.
UltimateOscillator.details:
## Description

`UltimateOscillator` (Larry Williams, 1976) combines the ratio of buying pressure to true range over three periods into one weighted oscillator, so that short, medium and long momentum enter a single value.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{BP}[t]   &= \text{close} - \min(\text{low},\ \text{close}_{t-1}) \\
\text{TR}[t]   &= \max(\text{high},\ \text{close}_{t-1}) - \min(\text{low},\ \text{close}_{t-1}) \\
\text{avg}_k   &= \frac{\sum \text{BP} \text{ over } \text{period}_k}{\sum \text{TR} \text{ over } \text{period}_k} \\
\text{UO}[t]   &= 100 \cdot \frac{4 \cdot \text{avg}_1 + 2 \cdot \text{avg}_2 + \text{avg}_3}{7}
\end{aligned}
$$

The 4 / 2 / 1 weighting puts the heaviest emphasis on the shortest period.

The inputs are `(high, low, close)`. The output lies in `[0, 100]` and is NaN until sample index `max(period1, period2, period3)`, following TA-Lib.


<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_START -->
## NaN handling

**Policy: `ignore`.** A `NaN` in any input gives a `NaN` output at that step. The step is skipped: it does not enter the window or update the internal state. See [NaN and warmup](../nan_and_warmup.md).
<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_END -->

WMA.name: WMA
WMA.title: Weighted Moving Average (WMA)

parameters.name: window_size
parameters.description: Number of most recent samples in the window; the newest sample gets weight window_size and the oldest weight 1.

parameters.name: start_policy
parameters.description: Output before the window is full: "strict" gives NaN, "expanding" computes from the samples seen so far, and "zero" treats the window as pre-filled with zeros.

WMA.details:
## Description

`WMA` computes the linearly weighted moving average: the most recent sample carries weight `w`, the one before it weight `w-1`, and so on down to weight `1` for the oldest sample in the window. The denominator is the triangular number `w*(w+1)/2`.

$$
\text{WMA}[t] = \frac{1 \cdot x[t-w+1] \;+\; 2 \cdot x[t-w+2] \;+\; \dots \;+\; w \cdot x[t]}{w \, (w+1) / 2}
$$

WMA is one of the three common moving averages, alongside `RollingMean` (SMA) and `EwMean` (EMA). `HullMA` is built from WMAs. The output before the window is full depends on `start_policy`, described under Warmup behavior below.

## Implementation Details

### Why O(1) per step?

WMA admits a closed-form rolling recurrence. Let `W[t] = 1·x[t-w+1] + ... + w·x[t]` be the linear-weighted sum, and `S[t-1]` the simple rolling sum of the *previous* window (i.e. `x[t-1] + x[t-2] + ... + x[t-w]`). Then

$$
W[t] - W[t-1] \;=\; w \cdot x[t] \;-\; S[t-1]
$$

(every old weight drops by 1, contributing `-S[t-1]`, and the new sample enters with weight `w`). `WMA` therefore keeps a rolling sum for `S` and a single number for `W`.

### Complexity

* Time complexity: `O(1)` per step.
* Space complexity: `O(window_size)` for the rolling-sum buffer.

### Warmup behavior

While the window is filling (n samples seen, `n < window_size`):

| Policy | Output during warmup |
|---|---|
| `"strict"` (default) | `NaN` |
| `"expanding"` | partial-window WMA: weights `1, 2, ..., n`, divisor `n(n+1)/2` |
| `"zero"` | weights `1, 2, ..., w` with implicit zeros for missing past, full divisor `w(w+1)/2` (output is dampened during warmup) |

The warmup numerators agree exactly when the window first fills, so the output is continuous at the switch to the recurrence.


<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_START -->
## NaN handling

**Policy: `ignore`.** A `NaN` in any input gives a `NaN` output at that step. The step is skipped: it does not enter the window or update the internal state. See [NaN and warmup](../nan_and_warmup.md).
<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_END -->

WilliamsR.name: WilliamsR
WilliamsR.title: Williams %R

parameters.name: window_size
parameters.description: Number of most recent bars over which the highest high and lowest low are taken.

references: Williams, L. (1979). *How I Made One Million Dollars Last Year Trading Commodities*. Windsor Books.
WilliamsR.details:
## Description

`WilliamsR` (Williams %R, by Larry Williams) returns the normalized position of the close within the recent (high, low) range, scaled to `[-100, 0]`:

$$
\%R[t] = -100 \cdot \frac{H_n[t] - C[t]}{H_n[t] - L_n[t]}
$$

where `H_n` and `L_n` are the rolling max of `high` and rolling min of `low` over the window. `%R = 0` means the close is at the period high, and `%R = -100` means the close is at the period low.

The inputs are `(high, low, close)`, in the order of TA-Lib's `WILLR`.

## Warmup and edge cases

The first `window_size - 1` outputs are NaN, so the first valid output is at sample index `window_size - 1`, following TA-Lib.

When `H_n == L_n` over the period (a flat segment), the formula is undefined and `WilliamsR` returns 0, matching TA-Lib.

## Implementation Details

The rolling high and low are kept in two monotonic deques, as in `RollingMin` and `RollingMax`.

* Time complexity: `O(1)` amortized per step.
* Space complexity: `O(window_size)`.

## Output shape

| You pass... | You get back... |
|---|---|
| three scalars `high, low, close` | `float` |
| three 1D arrays of shape `(T,)` | array of shape `(T,)` |
| three 2D arrays of shape `(T, K)` | array of shape `(T, K)`, column-by-column |
| three parallel iterables | `list[float]` (eager) |


<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_START -->
## NaN handling

**Policy: `ignore`.** A `NaN` in any input gives a `NaN` output at that step. The step is skipped: it does not enter the window or update the internal state. See [NaN and warmup](../nan_and_warmup.md).
<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_END -->

BandSignal.name: BandSignal
BandSignal.title: Entry and exit bands on a z-score
BandSignal.short: Three-state mean-reversion position from a z-score: short above +entry, long below -entry, flat again inside the exit level, with an optional stop and lockout.

parameters.name: entry
parameters.description: Entry level. A flat position goes short when the z-score reaches +entry and long when it reaches -entry.

parameters.name: exit
parameters.description: Exit level, in (-entry, entry). A short exits when the z-score falls to exit, a long when it rises to -exit.

parameters.name: stop
parameters.description: Stop level, above entry (inf = no stop). A short exits when the z-score reaches +stop, a long at -stop, and that side cannot re-enter until the z-score returns inside the exit level.

BandSignal.details:
## Description

`BandSignal(entry, exit, stop)(z)` turns a z-score into a position of `-1`, `0`,
or `+1` in a mean-reverting spread. The position is short (`-1`) when the
spread is high, because it is expected to fall, and long (`+1`) when it is low:

- Flat: go short when `z >= entry`, long when `z <= -entry`.
- Short: exit when `z <= exit`. Long: exit when `z >= -exit`.
- Stop: a short exits when `z >= stop` and a long when `z <= -stop`. That side
  is then locked until the z-score returns inside the exit level, so a spread
  that keeps diverging is not entered again at once. No entry is made beyond
  the stop.

The gap between the entry and exit levels is hysteresis: a z-score that hovers
near one level does not switch the position on and off. A negative `exit`
holds a position until the spread overshoots its mean. If the z-score jumps
from beyond one entry level to beyond the other in one step, the position
exits and enters the other side on that step.

Multiply the position by the leg sizes to get the targets of a pairs trade; see
the [portfolio backtest](../functions_fin/BacktestPortfolioTarget.md).

<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_START -->
## NaN handling

**Policy: `ignore`.** A `NaN` in any input gives a `NaN` output at that step. The step is skipped: it does not enter the window or update the internal state. See [NaN and warmup](../nan_and_warmup.md).
<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_END -->

Butter.details:
## Description

`Butter` is a causal IIR Butterworth low-pass filter of configurable order. The Butterworth design has a maximally flat frequency response in the passband and attenuates components above the cutoff. Higher filter orders give a steeper rolloff.

The digital filter is the bilinear transform of the analog Butterworth prototype, and matches `scipy.signal.butter(order, cutoff_freq)` followed by `scipy.signal.lfilter`.

## Description

Digital band-pass Butterworth IIR filter. Produces a 2N-order filter from the order-N analog prototype via the `lp2bp` transformation.

$$
\text{ButterBandpass}(N, W_{\text{low}}, W_{\text{high}})
$$

The pass band is `[low_cutoff, high_cutoff]`, as fractions of the Nyquist frequency. The output matches `scipy.signal.butter(order, [low, high], btype='bandpass')` followed by `scipy.signal.lfilter` to within about 1e-9.

import plotly.graph_objects as go
from screamer import ButterBandstop

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
fs = 500.0
N = 1000

# Composite: slow drift (3 Hz) + interference at 40 Hz + noise

CusumFilter.name: CusumFilter
CusumFilter.title: CUSUM event filter
CusumFilter.short: Symmetric CUSUM event filter: +1 when the cumulative rise since the last event passes a threshold, -1 for a fall, 0 otherwise.

parameters.name: threshold
parameters.description: Cumulative move, in the units of the input, that triggers an event. Must be positive.

parameters.name: drift
parameters.description: Amount subtracted from each rise and from each fall before it is accumulated, so moves smaller than `drift` per step do not build up. 0 or more.

references: Lopez de Prado, M. (2018). *Advances in Financial Machine Learning*, section 2.5.2.1. Wiley.
CusumFilter.details:
## Description

`CusumFilter` is the symmetric CUSUM event filter (Lopez de Prado 2018). It
keeps two running sums of the input,

$$
S^+_t = \max(0,\ S^+_{t-1} + x_t - \text{drift}), \qquad
S^-_t = \min(0,\ S^-_{t-1} + x_t + \text{drift}),
$$

and outputs `-1` when `S- < -threshold`, `+1` when `S+ > threshold`, and `0`
otherwise. After an event the sum that fired restarts from 0, as in the code of
the book (section 2.5.2.1). The other sum is not reset: a rise can only reach
the threshold after `S-` has climbed back to 0, and the reverse holds for a
fall, so the other sum is already 0 when an event occurs. The input is normally
returns or price differences, so an event marks a cumulative move of more than
`threshold` since the last event, in either direction.

The events are a sampling rule: label or trade only at the steps where the
output is not 0, for example with
[`TripleBarrier`](../functions_fin/TripleBarrier.md) entries at those steps.
To hold a position for a while after each event, follow it with
[`Hold`](Hold.md).

With `threshold=1`, the input `[0.5, 0.6, -0.2, 0.3, -1.5]` gives
`[0, 1, 0, 0, -1]`: the sum of the first two values passes 1, and after the
reset the fall to -1.5 passes -1.

<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_START -->
## NaN handling

**Policy: `ignore`.** A `NaN` in any input gives a `NaN` output at that step. The step is skipped: it does not enter the window or update the internal state. See [NaN and warmup](../nan_and_warmup.md).

CycleAmplitude.name: CycleAmplitude
CycleAmplitude.title: Instantaneous cycle amplitude
CycleAmplitude.short: Instantaneous amplitude (envelope) of the dominant cycle, scaled to the input amplitude.
references: Ehlers, J. F. (2001). *Rocket Science for Traders: Digital Signal Processing Applications*. Wiley.
CycleAmplitude.details:
## Description

`CycleAmplitude` reads the instantaneous amplitude, or envelope, of the
dominant cycle from John Ehlers' Hilbert transform. It is the magnitude
`sqrt(I^2 + Q^2)` of the `HilbertPhasor` pair. This follows Ehlers'
convention: he treats the magnitude of `(I1, Q1)` as the cycle amplitude in
price units, using `I1^2 + Q1^2` as the cycle power in the signal-to-noise
ratio of *Rocket Science for Traders*, and his factor `0.075 * period + 0.54`
corrects the Hilbert filter toward unit gain (the chapter is known here from
secondary sources, not from the book). That correction is approximate, so
screamer divides each component by its exact filter gain at the measured
period: a sine of amplitude `A` and any period from about 7 to 50 reads `A`.
It is a general envelope detector, tracking the local size of an oscillation
in the series, and applies to any sampled signal, not only price.

The scaling uses the measured period, so the reading is exact for a steady
cycle the engine measures correctly. At the short edge of the engine's range
it is not: a unit sine of period 6 reads about 1.6, because the engine
measures its period as about 18, and a cycle shorter than 6 samples is not
measured at all.

CyclePhase.name: CyclePhase
CyclePhase.title: Instantaneous cycle phase
CyclePhase.short: Instantaneous phase, in degrees, of Ehlers' in-phase and quadrature components.
references: Ehlers, J. F. (2001). *Rocket Science for Traders: Digital Signal Processing Applications*. Wiley.
CyclePhase.details:
## Description

`CyclePhase` reads the instantaneous phase of a series from John Ehlers'
Hilbert transform, in degrees, wrapped to `[0, 360)`. It is the angle
`atan2(Q1, I1)` of Ehlers' in-phase and quadrature components, the pair
`HilbertPhasor` returns before its scaling, and it uses the same engine as
`DominantCycle`. While the dominant cycle stays stable the phase
**decreases** by about `360 / period` degrees per sample, so it steps up by
360 once per cycle when it wraps. This is the direction of Ehlers' own phase
in MAMA, where the phase change `Phase[t-1] - Phase[t]` is positive on a
cycle. The estimate is a general spectral quantity: the same measurement
applies to any sampled signal, not only price.

`CycleSine` uses a different phase, the dominant cycle phase of Ehlers'
sinewave indicator, which increases with time.

<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_START -->

**Policy: `ignore`.** A `NaN` in any input gives a `NaN` output at that step. The step is skipped: it does not enter the window or update the internal state. See [NaN and warmup](../nan_and_warmup.md).

CycleSine.name: CycleSine
CycleSine.title: Cycle sinewave indicator
CycleSine.short: Ehlers' sinewave indicator (sine, leadsine) from the phase of the dominant cycle.
references: Ehlers, J. F. (2001). *Rocket Science for Traders: Digital Signal Processing Applications*. Wiley.
CycleSine.details:
## Description

`CycleSine` computes John Ehlers' sinewave indicator (*Rocket Science for
Traders*, "The Sinewave Indicator"), as TA-Lib implements it in `HT_SINE`.
`sine` is the sine of the dominant cycle phase, and `leadsine` is the same
curve advanced by 45 degrees, one eighth of a cycle. While the series cycles,
`sine` follows the cycle in phase and `leadsine` turns first, so the two
lines cross just before the cycle's peaks and troughs. When the series trends,
the phase stops rotating and the lines run apart without crossing.

The dominant cycle phase, `DCPhase`, comes from a Fourier sum over one cycle
of the smoothed price `s` (the 4-tap weighted mean the engine uses). `period`
is the dominant cycle period that `DominantCycle` reports, and `N` is that
period rounded to whole samples:

$$
\begin{aligned}
N &= \lfloor \text{period} + 0.5 \rfloor \\
R &= \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} \sin(360 k / N)\, s[t-k], \quad
I = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} \cos(360 k / N)\, s[t-k] \\
\text{DCPhase} &= \arctan(R / I) + 90 + 360 / \text{period}
  \;(+180 \text{ if } I < 0) \\
\text{sine} &= \sin(\text{DCPhase}), \quad
\text{leadsine} = \sin(\text{DCPhase} + 45)
\end{aligned}
$$

Angles are in degrees. The term `360 / period` compensates the one-sample
lag of the smoothing. `DCPhase` increases by about `360 / period` degrees per
sample, which is why `leadsine` leads. It is a different phase from
`CyclePhase`, which reads the angle of the `HilbertPhasor` pair and runs the
other way. The results agree with TA-Lib's `HT_SINE` once both have passed
their start-up transients.

The two outputs are stacked along a trailing axis of size 2: `out[..., 0]`
is `sine` and `out[..., 1]` is `leadsine`.

<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_START -->
## NaN handling

**Policy: `ignore`.** A `NaN` in any input gives a `NaN` output at that step. The step is skipped: it does not enter the window or update the internal state. See [NaN and warmup](../nan_and_warmup.md).

Decycler.details:
## Description

`Decycler` is a causal filter from John Ehlers that estimates the trend of a
series by removing its short cycles. It is the input minus its 1-pole highpass
component, so slow movements pass through and fast cycles are suppressed. The
cutoff is the half-power point: a cycle of exactly `period` samples keeps
about 71% of its amplitude (-3 dB), and cycles well below the cutoff are
removed.

The cutoff is set by a cycle length in samples (`period`) or a fraction of the
Nyquist frequency (`cutoff`), related by `cutoff = 2 / period`.

DominantCycle.short: Dominant cycle period via Ehlers' homodyne discriminator.
references: Ehlers, J. F. (2001). *Rocket Science for Traders: Digital Signal Processing Applications*. Wiley.
DominantCycle.details:
## Description

`DominantCycle` measures the dominant cycle period of a series, in samples,
using John Ehlers' homodyne discriminator. It forms the analytic signal by a
Hilbert transform, then reads the cycle period from the rate of change of the
phase between successive samples. The estimate is a general spectral quantity:
the same measurement applies to any sampled signal, not only price. It agrees
with TA-Lib's `HT_DCPERIOD`.

The period is limited to `[6, 50]` samples, as Ehlers publishes it: a longer
cycle reads 50 and a shorter one is not measured. A trend in the input biases
the estimate (a sine of period 10 on a steady ramp reads about 12), so Ehlers
measures cycles on detrended data. Pass a trending series through
`RoofingFilter` first.

<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_START -->

FracDiff.name: FracDiff
FracDiff.title: Fractional differentiation (FracDiff)
FracDiff.short: Fractional differencing filter. Removes the trend while keeping more of the series' memory than an integer difference.

parameters.name: d
parameters.description: Differencing order. 0 is the identity, 1 the first difference, 2 the second; negative values give fractional integration.

parameters.name: window_size
parameters.description: Maximum number of taps, which bounds memory and per-step cost.

parameters.name: threshold
parameters.description: Truncate the weight series at the first weight smaller than this in absolute value. 0.0 keeps all window_size taps.

parameters.name: start_policy
parameters.description: Output before the window is full: "strict" gives NaN, "expanding" computes from the samples seen so far, and "zero" treats the window as pre-filled with zeros.

references: López de Prado, M. (2018). *Advances in Financial Machine Learning*, chapter 5. Wiley.
Hosking, J. R. M. (1981). Fractional differencing. *Biometrika*, 68(1), 165-176. doi:10.1093/biomet/68.1.165
FracDiff.details:
## Description

`FracDiff` applies fractional differencing of order `d`: the filter whose taps are the binomial expansion of $(1-B)^d$, where $B$ is the backshift operator $Bx[t] = x[t-1]$.

$$
w_0 = 1, \qquad w_k = -w_{k-1}\,\frac{d - k + 1}{k}, \qquad y[t] = \sum_{k=0}^{L-1} w_k \, x[t-k]
$$

which is $w_k = (-1)^k \binom{d}{k}$.

Integer orders give the ordinary differences: `d=0` produces taps `[1]` and returns the input, `d=1` produces `[1, -1]` and equals [`Diff(1)`](../functions_misc/Diff.md), `d=2` produces `[1, -2, 1]` and equals [`Diff2`](../functions_misc/Diff2.md). At a fractional order the series does not terminate. Its weights decay as a power law, so `y[t]` keeps a weighted trace of the whole lookback rather than only the last one or two samples. That trace is the memory a first difference discards, and the reason to prefer `d = 0.4` over `d = 1` when the differenced series feeds a model that has something to learn from the level.

The order controls the trade: raise `d` toward 1 to remove more of the trend, lower it toward 0 to keep more memory.

## Implementation Details

### Truncation

The weight series is infinite for a fractional `d`, so the filter is truncated at

$$
L = \min\big(\text{window\_size},\ \text{first } k \text{ with } |w_k| < \text{threshold}\big)
$$

This is the fixed-width variant of Lopez de Prado (2018): the weights are truncated once, and the filter is applied at full width from then on. `window_size` bounds the cost, `threshold` removes taps too small to change the output. Both matter: at `d = 0.4` the weights fall below `1e-5` after a few hundred terms, while at `d = 0.05` they fall off far more slowly and `window_size` is what stops the filter.

`L` grows as `d` approaches 0 and shrinks as `d` approaches an integer, so the same `threshold` gives different filter lengths at different orders. Count the leading `NaN` values under `start_policy="strict"` to see the `L` a given configuration resolved to.

### Complexity

A circular buffer of the last `L` samples and one convolution sweep. **O(L) per step**, `O(L)` memory. The weights are computed once when the operator is constructed.

### Warmup behavior

`"strict"` (the default) returns `NaN` until `L` finite samples have arrived, which is the first index at which every tap has a sample to multiply.

`"expanding"` and `"zero"` both return the convolution over the samples seen so far. For a linear filter these two are the same arithmetic: using only the available samples is what padding the missing past with zeros produces, since the missing terms contribute zero either way. The early values are biased toward zero, and they are the values Lopez de Prado's fixed-width method discards.

See [NaN and warmup](../nan_and_warmup.md) for the full definition.

<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_START -->
## NaN handling

**Policy: `ignore`.** A `NaN` in any input gives a `NaN` output at that step. The step is skipped: it does not enter the window or update the internal state. See [NaN and warmup](../nan_and_warmup.md).
<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_END -->
