HilbertPhasor.name: HilbertPhasor
HilbertPhasor.title: Hilbert in-phase / quadrature components
HilbertPhasor.short: Ehlers' in-phase and quadrature components (TA-Lib HT_PHASOR), scaled to the input amplitude.
references: Ehlers, J. F. (2001). *Rocket Science for Traders: Digital Signal Processing Applications*. Wiley.
HilbertPhasor.details:
## Description

`HilbertPhasor` returns the in-phase and quadrature components `I1` and `Q1`
of John Ehlers' Hilbert transform (*Rocket Science for Traders*), the pair
TA-Lib returns from `HT_PHASOR`, from the same engine as `DominantCycle`. `I1`
is the detrended, smoothed input delayed by three samples, and `Q1` is its
Hilbert transform. `Q1` leads `I1` by a quarter cycle, Ehlers' convention.
Together they describe the instantaneous phase (`CyclePhase`) and amplitude
(`CycleAmplitude`) of the dominant cycle. The estimate is a general spectral
quantity: the same measurement applies to any sampled signal, not only price.

Scale: Ehlers treats the magnitude of `(I1, Q1)` as the cycle amplitude in
price units (his signal-to-noise ratio uses `I1^2 + Q1^2` as the cycle
power; known here from secondary sources) and corrects the Hilbert filter's
gain toward 1 with the factor `0.075 * period + 0.54`. The correction is
approximate, and TA-Lib returns the components with that approximate scale:
the magnitude for a unit sine is between about 0.71 and 1.04 for periods 7 to
50, and between 1.6 and 5.2 below 7. screamer keeps the convention's meaning
and makes the unit gain exact: it divides each component by its filter gain
at the measured period, so a sine of amplitude `A` and any period from about
7 to 50 gives components of amplitude `A`. At period 6 the engine misreads
the period (as about 18) and the components are too large. The phase relation and the shape match TA-Lib; the values
differ from `HT_PHASOR` by that per-period factor. With `w = 2 pi / period`
(the engine's period before its final smoothing) and `adj = 0.075 *
period[t-1] + 0.54`, the gains are

$$
\begin{aligned}
W &= \left| 0.4 + 0.3 e^{-iw} + 0.2 e^{-2iw} + 0.1 e^{-3iw} \right| \\
h &= 2\,\text{adj}\,(0.0962 \sin 3w + 0.5769 \sin w) \\
g_I &= W h, \qquad g_Q = W h^2
\end{aligned}
$$

and `inphase = I1 / g_I`, `quadrature = Q1 / g_Q`: `W` is the gain of the
4-tap price smoothing and `h` that of one pass of the Hilbert filter.

The two outputs are stacked along a trailing axis of size 2: `out[..., 0]`
is the in-phase component and `out[..., 1]` the quadrature component.

<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_START -->
## NaN handling

**Policy: `ignore`.** A `NaN` in any input gives a `NaN` output at that step. The step is skipped: it does not enter the window or update the internal state. See [NaN and warmup](../nan_and_warmup.md).
<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_END -->

Hold.name: Hold
Hold.title: Hold (time-latch operator)
Hold.short: Time-latch operator. Latches a nonzero finite input and holds it for n steps; returns the release value once the hold expires.

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: Number of steps the latched value is held, counting the trigger step: a nonzero input at t is output at t, t+1, ..., t+n-1.

parameters.name: release
parameters.description: Value returned when no hold is active and the input is zero. May be finite or NaN; inf is rejected.

parameters.name: cooldown
parameters.description: Steps after a hold expires in which nonzero inputs are ignored and the output is `release`. 0 turns it off.

Hold.details:
## Description

`Hold` latches a nonzero finite input and outputs it for `n` steps in total: the trigger step plus `n-1` continuation steps. When the hold expires and the next input is zero, the output returns to `release`. A new nonzero input during an active hold replaces the latched value and resets the counter to `n-1` remaining steps. A zero input means no trigger.

After a hold expires, nonzero inputs in the next `cooldown` steps are ignored and the output is `release`; a trigger during a hold still restarts it. A `NaN` step does not count as a cooldown step. With `n=2, cooldown=2`, the input `[5, 0, 7, 3, 0, 4, 0]` gives `[5, 5, 0, 0, 0, 4, 4]`: the triggers 7 and 3 fall in the cooldown.

$$
\text{output}[t] = \begin{cases}
\text{release} & \text{if cooldown} > 0 \text{ and remaining} = 0 \text{ (decrement cooldown)} \\\\
x[t] & \text{if } x[t] \neq 0 \text{ (latch; set remaining} = n-1\text{)} \\\\
\text{held} & \text{if } x[t] = 0 \text{ and remaining} > 0 \text{ (decrement remaining)} \\\\
\text{release} & \text{if } x[t] = 0 \text{ and remaining} = 0 \\\\
\text{NaN} & \text{if } x[t] = \text{NaN (state unchanged)}
\end{cases}
$$

When a hold ends, the cooldown counter is set to `cooldown`. `reset()` sets `remaining` and the cooldown counter to 0 and `held` to `release`.

## Implementation Details

O(1) per step. Three scalars of state: `cool` (cooldown steps left, initialized to 0), `held` (the most recently latched nonzero value, initialized to `release`) and `remaining` (steps left in the current hold, initialized to 0).


<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_START -->
## NaN handling

**Policy: `ignore`.** A `NaN` in any input gives a `NaN` output at that step. The step is skipped: it does not enter the window or update the internal state. See [NaN and warmup](../nan_and_warmup.md).
<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_END -->

InstantaneousTrendline.name: InstantaneousTrendline
InstantaneousTrendline.title: Instantaneous trendline
InstantaneousTrendline.short: Ehlers' instantaneous trendline, the mean over one measured dominant cycle.
references: Ehlers, J. F. (2001). *Rocket Science for Traders: Digital Signal Processing Applications*. Wiley.
InstantaneousTrendline.details:
## Description

`InstantaneousTrendline` is John Ehlers' instantaneous trendline (*Rocket
Science for Traders*, "The Instantaneous Trendline"), as TA-Lib implements it
in `HT_TRENDLINE`. It averages the input over one dominant cycle, measured at
every sample by the same Hilbert-transform engine as `DominantCycle`, then
smooths the average with a 4-tap weighted mean. An average over exactly one
cycle removes that cycle, so the trendline keeps the trend and drops the
dominant cycle.

$$
\begin{aligned}
N[t] &= \lfloor \text{period}[t] + 0.5 \rfloor \\
\text{itrend}[t] &= \frac{1}{N[t]} \sum_{k=0}^{N[t]-1} x[t-k] \\
\text{trendline}[t] &= \frac{4\,\text{itrend}[t] + 3\,\text{itrend}[t-1]
  + 2\,\text{itrend}[t-2] + \text{itrend}[t-3]}{10}
\end{aligned}
$$

`period` is the dominant cycle period in samples that `DominantCycle`
reports, limited to `[6, 50]`. The average costs lag: on a steady ramp the
trendline trails the price by `(N - 1) / 2 + 1` samples, half a cycle plus
one. A trend also biases the period estimate (see `DominantCycle`), and an
average over a cycle length that does not match the actual cycle leaves part
of the cycle in the output.

This is a parameterless function: the averaging window comes entirely from the
measured cycle.

<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_START -->
## NaN handling

**Policy: `ignore`.** A `NaN` in any input gives a `NaN` output at that step. The step is skipped: it does not enter the window or update the internal state. See [NaN and warmup](../nan_and_warmup.md).
<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_END -->

KalmanFilter.name: KalmanFilter
KalmanFilter.title: Scalar Kalman filter
KalmanFilter.short: Scalar 1-D Kalman filter for a noisy random-walk model.

parameters.name: process_var
parameters.description: Variance of the random-walk innovation. Larger values make the filter follow new measurements more closely, with a noisier output.

parameters.name: observation_var
parameters.description: Variance of the measurement noise. Must be positive.

parameters.name: initial_state
parameters.description: Starting state estimate x_0, used before the first observation.

parameters.name: initial_variance
parameters.description: Variance P_0 of the starting state. A large value such as 1e9 makes the filter forget the initial state quickly. inf is a diffuse prior, so the first observation sets the state, with the observation variance.

references: Kalman, R. E. (1960). A new approach to linear filtering and prediction problems. *Journal of Basic Engineering*, 82(1), 35-45. doi:10.1115/1.3662552
KalmanFilter.details:
## Description

Scalar 1-D Kalman filter for the "noisy random walk" model: state and observation are scalars with unit transition and observation matrices. It works as an adaptive smoother whose responsiveness is set by the ratio of process to observation noise.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{predict: } & x_\text{pred} = x_{t-1},\quad P_\text{pred} = P_{t-1} + \sigma^2_p \\
\text{gain: }    & K = P_\text{pred} / (P_\text{pred} + \sigma^2_o) \\
\text{update: }  & x_t = x_\text{pred} + K \cdot (z_t - x_\text{pred}) \\
                  & P_t = (1 - K) \cdot P_\text{pred}
\end{aligned}
$$

In the steady state $K$ converges to a constant determined by $\sigma^2_p / \sigma^2_o$, at which point the filter behaves like an exponential smoother with that effective $\alpha$.

## Implementation Details

Constant-time O(1) per step; no buffer, two scalar state variables (`x`, `P`).


<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_START -->
## NaN handling

**Policy: `ignore`.** A `NaN` in any input gives a `NaN` output at that step. The step is skipped: it does not enter the window or update the internal state. See [NaN and warmup](../nan_and_warmup.md).
<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_END -->

MAMA.name: MAMA
MAMA.title: MESA Adaptive Moving Average (MAMA)
MAMA.short: Ehlers' adaptive moving average pair (MAMA, FAMA), smoothing set by the rate of the cycle phase.

parameters.name: fast_limit
parameters.description: Upper bound on the smoothing constant, reached when the phase stalls or wraps.

parameters.name: slow_limit
parameters.description: Lower bound on the smoothing constant, reached when the phase changes by fast_limit / slow_limit degrees or more per sample.

references: Ehlers, J. F. (2001). MESA Adaptive Moving Averages. *Technical Analysis of Stocks & Commodities*, September 2001.
Ehlers, J. F. (2001). *Rocket Science for Traders: Digital Signal Processing Applications*. Wiley.
MAMA.details:
## Description

`MAMA` (MESA Adaptive Moving Average, John Ehlers, *Stocks & Commodities*,
September 2001, and *Rocket Science for Traders*) is an exponential moving
average whose smoothing constant changes every sample with the rate of the
cycle phase, as TA-Lib implements it in `MAMA`. The constant is `fast_limit`
divided by the phase change per sample. While a cycle of period `P` rotates
steadily the phase changes by about `360 / P` degrees per sample, so the
constant is small, about `fast_limit * P / 360`, and `MAMA` smooths heavily.
Where the phase stalls or wraps, the change drops to the 1-degree floor and
the constant jumps to `fast_limit`, so `MAMA` moves most of the way to the
price in one step. `FAMA` (following adaptive moving average) is a second pass
over `MAMA` at half the smoothing constant, and lags it.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Delta\phi[t]   &= \max\big(\phi[t-1] - \phi[t],\ 1\big) \\
\alpha[t]       &= \operatorname{clip}\!\left(\frac{\text{fast\_limit}}{\Delta\phi[t]},\ \text{slow\_limit},\ \text{fast\_limit}\right) \\
\text{MAMA}[t]  &= \alpha[t] \cdot x[t] + (1 - \alpha[t]) \cdot \text{MAMA}[t-1] \\
\text{FAMA}[t]  &= 0.5\,\alpha[t] \cdot \text{MAMA}[t] + (1 - 0.5\,\alpha[t]) \cdot \text{FAMA}[t-1]
\end{aligned}
$$

$\phi$ is Ehlers' phase $\arctan(Q_1 / I_1)$ in degrees, from the in-phase and
quadrature components of the Hilbert transform (`HilbertPhasor`), taken as 0
when $I_1 = 0$. It lies in $(-90, 90)$, so it wraps every half cycle and
`alpha` steps to `fast_limit` twice per cycle. The phase change $\Delta\phi$
is floored at 1 degree so `alpha` never exceeds `fast_limit`. `MAMA` and
`FAMA` are both seeded with the first input after the warm-up.

The two outputs are stacked along a trailing axis of size 2: `out[..., 0]`
is `MAMA` and `out[..., 1]` is `FAMA`.

The results agree with TA-Lib's `MAMA` once its start-up has faded (TA-Lib
starts both averages at 0).

<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_START -->
## NaN handling

**Policy: `ignore`.** A `NaN` in any input gives a `NaN` output at that step. The step is skipped: it does not enter the window or update the internal state. See [NaN and warmup](../nan_and_warmup.md).
<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_END -->

MovingAverage.name: MovingAverage
MovingAverage.title: FIR moving average (arbitrary taps)

parameters.name: taps
parameters.description: FIR coefficients; taps[0] multiplies the current sample and taps[-1] the oldest. Must be non-empty. The default is a 3-tap triangular kernel.

MovingAverage.details:
## Description

Finite-impulse-response (FIR) filter with arbitrary user-supplied tap coefficients:

$$
y[t] = \sum_{k=0}^{L-1} \text{taps}[k] \cdot x[t - k]
$$

`taps[0]` is the coefficient on the *current* sample; `taps[L-1]` is on the oldest. Pre-compute the coefficient vector with `numpy` (`np.hamming(n)`, `np.bartlett(n)`, `np.blackman(n)`, `np.kaiser(n, beta)`) or `scipy.signal.firwin` and pass it in. The taps are used as given, so normalize them yourself if you need unity gain (for example, divide by `taps.sum()` for a low-pass smoother).

The first `len(taps) - 1` outputs are `NaN`.

## Implementation Details

Circular buffer of the last `L = len(taps)` samples plus an in-order convolution sweep. **O(L) per step**.


<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_START -->
## NaN handling

**Policy: `ignore`.** A `NaN` in any input gives a `NaN` output at that step. The step is skipped: it does not enter the window or update the internal state. See [NaN and warmup](../nan_and_warmup.md).
<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_END -->

RoofingFilter.name: RoofingFilter
RoofingFilter.title: Ehlers roofing filter (bandpass)
RoofingFilter.short: Ehlers bandpass, a highpass then a SuperSmoother.

parameters.name: hp_period
parameters.description: Highpass cutoff as a cycle length in samples; longer cycles (the trend) are removed. Give exactly one of hp_period and hp_cutoff. The default shown is a suggested starting value; the constructor has no default.

parameters.name: lp_period
parameters.description: Lowpass cutoff as a cycle length in samples; shorter cycles (noise) are removed. Give exactly one of lp_period and lp_cutoff. The default shown is a suggested starting value; the constructor has no default.

parameters.name: hp_cutoff
parameters.description: Highpass cutoff as a fraction of the Nyquist frequency, in (0, 1), equal to 2 / hp_period. Give exactly one of hp_period and hp_cutoff.

parameters.name: lp_cutoff
parameters.description: Lowpass cutoff as a fraction of the Nyquist frequency, in (0, 1), equal to 2 / lp_period. Give exactly one of lp_period and lp_cutoff.

references: Ehlers, J. F. (2013). *Cycle Analytics for Traders: Advanced Technical Trading Concepts*. Wiley.
Ehlers, J. F. (2014). Predictive and successful indicators. *Technical Analysis of Stocks & Commodities*, 32(1), 16-25, January 2014.
RoofingFilter.details:
## Description

`RoofingFilter` is a causal bandpass from John Ehlers. It applies a 2-pole
highpass at `hp_period` to remove the trend, then a `SuperSmoother` at
`lp_period` to remove fast noise, leaving the band of cycles between the two
cutoffs. It is the preprocessing step Ehlers applies before measuring a cycle,
because a raw series carries a trend and high-frequency noise that distort the
measurement.

Each cutoff is a cycle length in samples (`hp_period`, `lp_period`) or a fraction
of the Nyquist frequency (`hp_cutoff`, `lp_cutoff`), related by `cutoff = 2 / period`.

<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_START -->
## NaN handling

**Policy: `ignore`.** A `NaN` in any input gives a `NaN` output at that step. The step is skipped: it does not enter the window or update the internal state. See [NaN and warmup](../nan_and_warmup.md).
<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_END -->

SchmittTrigger.name: SchmittTrigger
SchmittTrigger.title: Schmitt trigger (hysteresis comparator)
SchmittTrigger.short: Hysteresis comparator. Latches 1.0 above the upper threshold, 0.0 below the lower threshold, and retains its previous value in between.

parameters.name: lower
parameters.description: Lower threshold, finite. The output latches to 0.0 when the input falls strictly below this value.

parameters.name: upper
parameters.description: Upper threshold, finite and strictly greater than lower. The output latches to 1.0 when the input rises strictly above this value.

parameters.name: initial
parameters.description: Latch value held before the first threshold crossing. Must be 0.0 (low), 1.0 (high), or NaN (undefined until the first crossing). Defaults to 0.0, so a signal that starts inside the dead band reads low rather than NaN.

references: Schmitt, O. H. (1938). A thermionic trigger. *Journal of Scientific Instruments*, 15(1), 24-26.
SchmittTrigger.details:
## Description

`SchmittTrigger` is a hysteresis comparator with two thresholds. The output switches to 1.0 when the input rises above the upper threshold and to 0.0 when it falls below the lower threshold; between the two thresholds the output holds its previous value. Because both thresholds must be crossed in opposite directions to produce a state change, a signal that wanders within the dead band does not affect the output.

$$
\text{output}[t] = \begin{cases}
1.0 & \text{if } x[t] > \text{upper} \\\\
0.0 & \text{if } x[t] < \text{lower} \\\\
\text{output}[t-1] & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$

The window `[lower, upper]` is the *dead band*. Inside it the output is latched: whichever value (1.0 or 0.0) the trigger last committed to is held until the input crosses out the other side.

Until the first input crosses either threshold the output holds the `initial` latch seed. The default is `0.0` (the low state), so a signal that starts inside the dead band reads low rather than `NaN`. Pass `initial=1.0` to start high, or `initial=nan` to leave the output undefined until the first crossing.

## Implementation Details

O(1) per step. One scalar of state (the latched output). The constructor rejects `lower >= upper`, non-finite thresholds, and an `initial` that is not `0.0`, `1.0`, or `nan`; `reset()` restores the latched state to `initial`.


<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_START -->
## NaN handling

**Policy: `ignore`.** A `NaN` in any input gives a `NaN` output at that step. The step is skipped: it does not enter the window or update the internal state. See [NaN and warmup](../nan_and_warmup.md).
<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_END -->

import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go

from screamer import SchmittTrigger

# A noisy sine wave that repeatedly crosses zero.

x = np.sin(t) + 0.25 * np.random.default_rng(0).standard_normal(400)

# A naive zero-cross comparator would chatter on the noise. The
# Schmitt trigger requires the signal to swing past +/- 0.3 before
# toggling, so it produces a clean square wave.

y = trig(x)

fig.add_hline(y=-0.3, line_dash='dash', line_color='gray', row=1, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(y=y, mode='lines', name='trigger',
                         line=dict(color='red')),             row=2, col=1)
fig.update_layout(
    title="Schmitt trigger on a noisy sine wave (lower=-0.3, upper=+0.3)",
    xaxis2_title="Sample", yaxis=dict(title="Input"),

SuperSmoother.name: SuperSmoother
SuperSmoother.title: Ehlers SuperSmoother lowpass filter

parameters.name: period
parameters.description: Cutoff as a cycle length in samples; cycles shorter than this are attenuated. Give exactly one of period and cutoff. The default shown is a suggested starting value; the constructor has no default.

parameters.name: cutoff
parameters.description: Cutoff as a fraction of the Nyquist frequency, in (0, 1), equal to 2 / period. Give exactly one of period and cutoff.

references: Ehlers, J. F. (2013). *Cycle Analytics for Traders: Advanced Technical Trading Concepts*. Wiley.
SuperSmoother.details:
## Description

`SuperSmoother` is a causal 2-pole IIR lowpass filter from John Ehlers. It passes
components of the input series slower than the cutoff and attenuates faster ones,
with less lag and less ringing than a Butterworth filter of comparable rolloff.

The cutoff is set by a cycle length in samples (`period`) or, equivalently, a
fraction of the Nyquist frequency (`cutoff`), related by `cutoff = 2 / period`.
The filter coefficients follow Ehlers' critically damped design.

<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_START -->
## NaN handling

**Policy: `ignore`.** A `NaN` in any input gives a `NaN` output at that step. The step is skipped: it does not enter the window or update the internal state. See [NaN and warmup](../nan_and_warmup.md).
<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_END -->

TrendMode.name: TrendMode
TrendMode.title: Trend-vs-cycle classifier
TrendMode.short: Ehlers' trend mode, 1.0 while the series trends and 0.0 while it cycles.
references: Ehlers, J. F. (2001). *Rocket Science for Traders: Digital Signal Processing Applications*. Wiley.
TrendMode.details:
## Description

`TrendMode` classifies each sample of a series as trending (`1.0`) or
cycling (`0.0`) with John Ehlers' rule from *Rocket Science for Traders*
("Identifying Market Modes"), as TA-Lib implements it in `HT_TRENDMODE`. It
combines three measurements of the dominant cycle: the sinewave indicator
(`CycleSine`), the rate of its phase, and the instantaneous trendline
(`InstantaneousTrendline`).

Each sample starts as trend, then:

1. A crossing of `sine` and `leadsine` marks a cycle turn. That sample reads
   cycle, and so does every sample until half a dominant period has passed
   since the last crossing.
2. A phase that advances between 0.67 and 1.5 times `360 / period` degrees per
   sample (the dominant cycle rotating at its own rate) reads cycle.
3. A smoothed price at least 1.5% away from the trendline,
   `|smooth - trendline| >= 0.015 |trendline|`, reads trend whatever rules
   1 and 2 say.

Rule 3 compares the price with the trendline in relative terms, so it is
meant for price series, which stay well away from zero. On a series that
oscillates around zero, such as returns or a detrended signal, the trendline
is close to zero and every sample reads trend. For the same reason a cycle
whose swing exceeds about 1.5% of the price reads trend near its peaks and
troughs, where the price runs furthest from the trendline: a cycle of
amplitude 3 on a level of 100 reads cycle on only about half the samples.
There are no settings: the thresholds are Ehlers'.

<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_START -->
## NaN handling

**Policy: `ignore`.** A `NaN` in any input gives a `NaN` output at that step. The step is skipped: it does not enter the window or update the internal state. See [NaN and warmup](../nan_and_warmup.md).
<!-- NAN_FOOTNOTE_END -->

import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go

rng = np.random.default_rng(20)

cycle_part = 100 + np.sin(2 * np.pi * np.arange(c) / 20)    # 300 samples of a 20-sample cycle around 100
ramp_part = cycle_part[-1] + 0.1 * np.arange(1, c + 1)        # then 300 samples of a straight ramp
x = np.concatenate([cycle_part, ramp_part]) + 0.01 * rng.standard_normal(2 * c)

mode = TrendMode()(x)

fig = make_subplots(rows=2, cols=1, shared_xaxes=True, row_heights=[0.7, 0.3], vertical_spacing=0.06)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(y=x, name='cycle, then ramp', line=dict(color='gray')), row=1, col=1)

                         line=dict(color='darkorange', shape='hv')), row=2, col=1)

CombineLatest.name: CombineLatest
CombineLatest.title: CombineLatest
CombineLatest.short: As-of latest-value join of N streams: one row per distinct index (same-index events coalesce).
CombineLatest.details:
An as-of join for streams that tick on different clocks. It aligns N streams by
carrying each input's most recent value forward and emitting **one row per
distinct index** - same-index events from multiple streams coalesce into a
single settled row. `emit="when_all"` (default) waits until every input is warm;
`emit="on_any"` starts from the first event.

Delay.name: Delay
Delay.title: Delay
Delay.short: Re-stamp each event's index by a fixed time offset (a latency line).
Delay.details:
`Delay(duration)` shifts every event's index by `duration` (in index units) and
leaves its value unchanged: event `(t, v)` becomes `(t + duration, v)`. It is the
time-based counterpart of `Lag`, which shifts by a fixed number of events. On a
regular grid the two coincide (`duration = N * step` equals `Lag(N)`); on an
irregular feed `Delay` shifts by wall-time and `Lag` shifts by event count.

The shift is lossless, one output per input, order-preserving, and starts `duration`
late (no NaN warmup). `duration` is numeric in index units (a millisecond index uses
`Delay(600_000)` for a 10-minute delay); there is no calendar parsing.

`Delay` requires an explicit index (there is nothing to shift against without one);
calling it on a bare array is a `TypeError`.

## Parameters

- `duration`: the index offset to add to every event, numeric, in index units.

## Delay inside a Pipeline merge

A `Delay` feeding a `CombineLatest` merge inside a single compiled `Pipeline` is now
correct in both batch and live modes. Before the fix, the merge received delayed frames
too early because the batch merge sorted raw inputs before the delay re-stamped their
indices; batch and live agreed, but both produced lookahead results.

The fix introduces a bounded reorder buffer inside the fused merge. Frames with a
future-dated index are held in the buffer and released in global index order once every
per-port watermark has advanced past them. When a sibling stream is idle, `advance(now)`
releases buffered rows so the merge does not wait for a stalled input. A genuinely stalled
stream trips the reorder cap (`max_pending`, default 1,000,000) and raises a `RuntimeError`
with a clear message.

The `forecast_pairs` / separate-call pattern continues to work unchanged.

import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from screamer import Delay

idx = np.array([0, 7, 14, 21, 28], dtype=np.int64)
vals = np.array([1.0, 3.0, 2.0, 4.0, 3.5])
dv, di = Delay(5)(vals, idx)

fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=idx, y=vals, mode="lines+markers", name="input"))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=di, y=dv, mode="lines+markers", name="Delay(5)"))
fig.update_layout(title="Delay shifts the index by 5 units",
                  xaxis_title="index", yaxis_title="value",
                  margin=dict(l=20, r=20, t=50, b=20))
fig.show()

Dropna.name: Dropna
Dropna.title: Dropna
Dropna.short: Drop events whose value is NaN.
Dropna.details:
Drop events whose value is `NaN`. This changes the length of the stream (it is a
cardinality-changing stream operator, unlike the shape-preserving compute
functors). Usable eagerly and inside a `Pipeline`.

Feeding a lazy iterator of `(value, index)` pairs returns a lazy iterator of the surviving events; feeding arrays or `(values, index)` tuples returns the batch result.

Each argument is one stream; an index goes in a `(values, index)` tuple (or
`index=` for one array). Several streams merge in index order, ties in argument
order, and each event is dropped on its own, as the `Dropna` node of a
`Pipeline` given several streams does: `Dropna()(a, b)` with `a` and `b` arrays
or tuples is that node.

Filter.name: Filter
Filter.title: Filter
Filter.short: Two-input mask gate that keeps each data value whose aligned mask is nonzero.
Filter.details:
A 2-input mask gate: keep each data value whose aligned mask value is nonzero
(zero or NaN drops, any other value keeps). The mask is an ordinary stream
built from upstream comparison or logic ops. No Python predicate or callback -
the gate logic runs entirely in C++ for batch, lazy, and graph regimes.

Gate rule: `mask == 0` or `isnan(mask)` drops the aligned data value; any
other mask value (positive, negative, non-NaN) keeps it. A NaN data value
passes through unmodified when its aligned mask is nonzero.

The data and the mask are one column each. A wider data or mask stream raises
`ValueError` before any event is fed; select the column to gate first, for
example `Filter()(Select(columns=[0])(data), mask)`.

Merge.name: Merge
Merge.title: Merge
Merge.short: Merge N value streams into one index-sorted (values, sources, index).
Merge.details:
Interleave several streams into one index-sorted stream, tagging each event with
the integer index of the source it came from. This is the causal, order-preserving
way to fan several streams into a single timeline.

Resample.name: Resample
Resample.title: Resample
Resample.short: Causal windowed downsample of a 1-D or multi-column value stream.
Resample.details:
Causal windowed downsampling. Group a stream into fixed index-interval buckets
(`freq=`) or fixed event-count buckets (`count=`), reduce each bucket with a
per-bar aggregation, and return a `(values, index)` tuple. A bucket emits only once a
later index proves it complete; the trailing partial bucket emits at end of input.
Usable eagerly (raw arrays or `(values, index)` tuples) and inside a `Pipeline`.

Feeding a lazy iterator of `(value, index)` pairs returns a lazy iterator of bar events; feeding arrays or `(values, index)` tuples returns the batch result.

The `agg` parameter accepts two forms:

**String shorthand**: one of `first`, `last`, `min`, `max`, `sum`, `count`,
`mean`, `ohlc`, `ohlcv`, `ohlcv2`, `ohlc_bars`, `ohlcv_bars`. `ohlc` returns
four columns (`open`, `high`, `low`, `close`). With `freq=`, `count=` or
`clock=True`, the aggs `first` to `ohlc` aggregate every column of a
multi-column input separately: `mean` turns `(T, X)` into `(T', X)`, and `ohlc`
appends the four bar columns as a last axis, `(T', X, 4)`. The bar aggs
`ohlcv`, `ohlcv2`, `ohlc_bars`, and `ohlcv_bars` read the columns of a 2-D
input as the fields of one bar; see below. All multi-column aggs give the same
numbers in eager, `Pipeline` graph, and lazy iterator regimes. A
`threshold=` resample takes one value column.

Inside a `Pipeline`, a stream holds flat rows, so `ohlc` on `X` columns gives
`(T', 4 * X)`. The columns are in column-major field order, the four bar
fields of column 0 first: `[open_0, high_0, low_0, close_0, open_1, ...]`.
`values.reshape(len(values), X, 4)` gives the eager `(T', X, 4)` result. This
holds in every mode (`freq=`, `count=`, `clock=True`), in batch, lazy and
live runs, and in JavaScript. Phase 2 of the shape contract (asset axes
inside a `Pipeline`) will return `(T', X, 4)` directly.

**Any `EvalOp` functor**, e.g. `ExpandingSkew()`. The functor is `reset()` at
each bar boundary and fed every in-bar sample; its last output before the close
is emitted as the bar value. All screamer functors are valid reducers. A
functor aggregates one column, and a multi-column input raises `ValueError`.

**Several reducers at once**: run one `Resample` per statistic over the same
bucketing and align the results with `CombineLatest`. Because every `Resample`
shares the same `freq=` (or `count=`) and clock, the bars line up exactly and
cannot drift, e.g.
`CombineLatest()(Resample(freq=5, agg="first")(price, t), Resample(freq=5, agg="sum")(vol, t))`.
Inside a `Pipeline`, place each per-stat `Resample` node on its upstream expression
and combine them the same way; per-tick transforms live in the expression, e.g.
`Resample(freq=5, agg=ExpandingSum())(PosPart()(vol))`.

## Bucketing: `freq=` vs `count=`

Exactly one of `freq=` or `count=` sets how bars are bounded, and they answer
different questions.

- `freq=W` buckets along the **index**. Bar `n` is the half-open interval
  `[origin + n*W, origin + (n+1)*W)`, so the index values decide membership. Bars
  have equal width on the index but a variable number of ticks; a tick exactly on a
  boundary starts the later bar. Boundaries are anchored at `origin` (default `0`,
  i.e. multiples of `W`), **not** at the first tick. Set `origin=` to shift the
  grid. Internal empty intervals are real and controlled by `fill=`.
- `count=N` buckets by **arrival order**. A bar closes every `N` events and never
  consults the index values to place boundaries. Bars have an equal number of ticks
  but a variable width on the index, and one bar can straddle an arbitrary index gap
  without noticing it.

The `index` argument is **optional in both modes**. `count=` does not need it to
find boundaries; `freq=` uses it as the timeline being bucketed. If omitted, row
position (`0, 1, 2, ...`) is used as the index.

Bar **labels** depend on the mode and on `label=`:

- `freq=`: the bar's **grid edge**, `origin + n*W` for `label="left"` (default)
  or `origin + (n+1)*W` for `label="right"`. This is the interval boundary itself,
  which need not equal any actual tick's index (and a right label can sit past the
  last tick).
- `count=`: an **actual tick index**, the **first** tick of the bar for
  `label="left"` or the **last** for `label="right"`.

Concretely, eight ticks at index `[0, 1, 2, 10, 11, 20, 21, 22]`:

- `freq=10` -> bars `{0,1,2} {10,11} {20,21,22}` (counts 3, 2, 3), labels
  `[0, 10, 20]` (grid edges).
- `count=3`  -> bars `{0,1,2} {10,11,20} {21,22}` (counts 3, 3, 2), labels
  `[0, 10, 21]` (first tick of each bar). The middle bar straddles the `11 -> 20`
  gap because `count=` measures rows, not index distance.

## Empty buckets: `fill=`

`fill=` controls what happens when a `freq=` bar contains no samples (an index
interval with no ticks). It applies to eager arrays, `(values, index)` tuples, and graphs alike;
it is not `Pipeline`-only.

- `"skip"` (default): emit no row for an empty bucket (the legacy behavior).
- `"nan"`: emit an all-NaN row at the empty bucket's label.
- `"carry"`: each column takes its last non-NaN value. An empty bucket repeats
  those values, and a NaN cell of a bar (a column with no finite value in the
  bucket) takes its column's value, as a forward fill of each column would.
  A column without a value yet stays NaN.

Only **internal** empty buckets (gaps between two events) are filled by `Resample`
itself. Trailing empty buckets after the last event are not synthesized here; that
needs a clock, via either [`pipe.live().advance(now)`](#pipeline-live) or a clock input
wired into a `Pipeline`. The [`pipe.live()` reference](#pipeline-live) has a worked example.
Inside a `Pipeline`, rows that a `Dropna` or `Filter` drops move time forward as
`advance()` does: a bucket they pass is closed, and filled when empty. At the end of
the input the open bucket is emitted only if it has data, so a `Dropna`, a `Filter`
and a `CombineLatest` that drop the same last rows give the same bars.

`fill=` applies under `freq=` (`every=`) and `clock=`. A `count=` bar holds `N`
events and a `threshold=` bar holds the events that reach the threshold, so
neither is ever empty, and `fill="nan"` or `"carry"` with them raises
`ValueError` (`RangeError` in JavaScript).

`max_fill=` (default 1,000,000) bounds the empty bars of one gap: the empty
buckets that one event, or one `advance(now)`, closes at once. A larger gap
raises `ValueError` (`RangeError` in JavaScript, where the option is `maxFill`)
before any bar is built, in batch, lazy and live calls alike. A gap that large
is usually a unit mistake, such as a nanosecond index with `freq=10`, and filling
it would exhaust memory. One fill bar costs at least 16 bytes in the graph and
about as much again in the result, so the default keeps one gap near 32 MB for
one column; it covers 11 days of one-second bars or 1.9 years of one-minute
bars. Pass a larger integer, up to 2\*\*53, to fill longer gaps.
The limit counts one step, so a live session that calls `advance(now)` in small
steps fills a gap that a batch call over the same events rejects. A rejected
`advance(now)` leaves the session usable; later events must still come at or
after `now`.

### `fill=` edge cases

- **Leading buckets** (before the first event) are never synthesized on the eager
  path: output starts at the bucket containing the first tick. A tick at index 47
  with `freq=10` starts at label 40, not 0. Leading empty buckets arise only from a
  clock (a `Pipeline` clock input or [`advance()`](#pipeline-live)) that advances time before
  the first data event; there `"nan"` emits NaN rows and `"carry"` **skips** them,
  since there is no previous row to repeat.
- **`"carry"` works per column** and treats every column alike, including
  count-like or sum-like columns: a genuinely empty bar carries the previous
  bar's count, not 0. Use `"nan"` where that is wrong for your columns. A wide
  input, `(T, K)`, gives the same values as `K` separate one-column calls.
  3.0.0 changed this: 2.8.0 repeated the previous row as it was, NaN cells
  included, and under `freq=` kept a bar whose events were all NaN as a NaN
  bar. For the 2.8.0 values, resample with `fill="nan"` and forward-fill only
  the rows of empty buckets.
- **`label="right"`** composes with `fill=` unchanged: a filled bucket is labelled at
  its right grid edge, like any other bar.
- **Functor reducers** are unaffected. A filled empty bucket emits a synthetic row
  (a NaN row, or the carried row) without feeding or resetting the reducer; the
  reducer is `reset()` only at the next real bar boundary. An expanding reducer
  therefore starts each real bar clean and never accumulates across a filled gap.

## Output format and column order

Every `Resample` call returns a `(values, index)` tuple. Unpack it as
`values, index = Resample(...)(data, idx)`. Multi-column aggregations (`ohlc`,
`ohlcv`, `ohlcv2`, `ohlc_bars`, `ohlcv_bars`) return a 2-D values array; columns
are positional in documented order. Use
`to_pandas(values, index, columns=["open","high","low","close"])` to attach names
for display. See [OHLC column order](Stream.md#ohlc-column-order) for the full
column listing.

## `ohlcv` and `ohlcv2` (two-column input)

Both require `values` to be a `(T, 2)` array: column 0 is price, column 1 is
volume (unsigned for `ohlcv`, signed for `ohlcv2`). Both work in eager, graph,
and lazy regimes.

`ohlcv` produces `(open, high, low, close, volume)`. The volume column is the sum
of column-1 values inside each bar.

`ohlcv2` produces `(open, high, low, close, buy_vol, sell_vol)`. Buy volume is
`sum(max(v, 0))` and sell volume is `sum(|min(v, 0)|)` per bar (both non-negative),
the signed-part decomposition of the column-1 signed volume.

## `ohlc_bars` (re-aggregate pre-built OHLC bars)

`ohlc_bars` compresses already-built OHLC bars into wider bars. It requires a
`(T, 4)` input: columns are `[open, high, low, close]`. The bar re-aggregation
applies `first` to column 0, `max` to column 1, `min` to column 2, and `last` to
column 3, preserving the OHLC interpretation across bar boundaries. Both `freq=`
and `count=` bucketing work; the agg is supported in eager, graph, and lazy
regimes without restriction.

## `ohlcv_bars` (re-aggregate pre-built OHLCV bars)

`ohlcv_bars` compresses OHLCV bars with one or more volume columns. It requires a
`(T, N)` input with `N >= 5`: columns `[open, high, low, close, vol1, vol2, ...]`.
The first four columns reduce as in `ohlc_bars`; every trailing column is summed.
Output shape is `(bars, N)`. The number of trailing volume columns may vary freely;
the plan is resolved from the actual input width at runtime. Supported in eager,
graph, and lazy regimes.

## `threshold=`: cumulative-driver (information bars)

`threshold=T` is the fourth mutually exclusive mode selector. A bar closes when
the cumulative sum of a **driver** stream since the last close reaches `T`. The
observation that crosses the threshold is included in the closing bar; then the
driver accumulator resets to 0.

Typical use: volume bars (each bar contains exactly `T` units of traded volume),
dollar bars (each bar contains `T` notional), or imbalance bars where the driver
is a signed trade-flow measure. Call as
`values, index = Resample(price_vi, driver, threshold=T, agg='ohlc')`.

- `price_vi` is a `(values, index)` tuple (or a bare array with a separate
  index). It supplies the bar's value stream and the time axis.
- `driver` is a 1-D array of the same length as `price_vi`. It is the per-event
  driver that accumulates toward `T`.
- `threshold=T` must be `> 0` (raises `ValueError` otherwise).
- `threshold=` is mutually exclusive with `freq=`, `every=`, and `count=`; passing
  two mode selectors raises `ValueError`.
- A `NaN` or infinite driver value is **ignored**: it does not advance the cumulative sum, and
  the clock does not move. The observation's value **does** contribute to the bar's
  reducer (the bar boundary is not affected by the NaN, but the price is still
  accumulated).
- Bar labels: by default (`label="left"`) each bar's index is the actual index of
  the first event in that bar. With `label="right"` it is the index of the last
  event (the crossing observation).
- The trailing partial bar (events since the last close, before cumulative driver
  reaches `T`) is always emitted at end of input.
- `threshold=` supports builtin string aggs only:
  `first`, `last`, `min`, `max`, `sum`, `count`, `mean`, `ohlc`.
  `ohlc` is accepted because it builds 4 output columns from 1 value column.
  Functor aggs (`ExpandingSkew()`, ...) raise `ValueError`; apply the functor
  downstream on the per-bar output instead.
  The multi-column-value aggs `ohlcv`, `ohlcv2`, `ohlc_bars`, and `ohlcv_bars`
  require a 2-D or wider value input that is not available in `threshold=` mode
  and also raise `ValueError`. To build OHLCV volume bars, resample the OHLC and
  the volume separately with `agg='ohlc'` and `agg='sum'` and combine with
  `CombineLatest`.
- Works in eager, `Pipeline` graph, and lazy iterator regimes with identical results.

**Graph regime.** Wire two `Input` nodes, one for the value stream and one for
the driver, then call `Resample(value_node, driver_node, threshold=T, agg=...)`.
For example: `x = Input('price'); d = Input('driver');
node = Resample(x, d, threshold=500, agg='ohlc');
dag = Pipeline([x, d], [node]);
ohlc, bar_idx = dag((price_arr, idx), (volume_arr, idx))`.

## `clock=True`: target-clock (as-of join)

`clock=True` is the fifth mode selector. A bar closes at each event of a separate
**clock** stream rather than at a fixed index interval, event count, or driver
threshold. The bar accumulates value events with index in `(previous_tick, tick]`
and emits at the clock tick.

The canonical use is an **as-of join**: emit the last known value of one stream as
of each event of another (the "clock" or "observation" stream). With `agg='last'`
and `fill='carry'`, the output carries the most-recent value forward to every clock
tick, even if the value stream has been silent since the previous tick.

Call as `values, index = Resample(value_vi, clock_vi, clock=True, agg='last', fill='carry')`.

For a freshness-bounded as-of join, add `max_age=N`, where `N` is an integer
number of index units. It is deliberately limited to scalar
`clock=True, agg='last', fill='carry'` joins: at a clock tick, the latest finite
source value is used only when `tick_index - source_index <= max_age`. Once an
observed source value expires, the clock row is emitted as NaN; a later finite
value resumes the join. `max_age=None` (the default) preserves unbounded carry.

- `value_vi` is a `(values, index)` tuple (or a bare array with a separate index).
  It supplies the stream being resampled.
- `clock_vi` is a `(clock_values, clock_index)` tuple. Its **index** drives bar
  boundaries; the clock values themselves are ignored.
- `agg=` accepts the same builtin string aggs as the other modes (`first`, `last`,
  `min`, `max`, `sum`, `count`, `mean`, `ohlc`). Functor aggs raise `ValueError`
  with `clock=`; apply the functor downstream on the per-bar output instead.
  `fill='carry'` gives each column its last non-NaN value at a clock tick
  whose bar has no finite value in that column, as under `freq=`;
  `fill='skip'` (the default) suppresses emission at empty-bucket clock ticks.
- `clock=True` is mutually exclusive with `freq=`, `every=`, `count=`, and
  `threshold=`; passing two mode selectors raises `ValueError`.
- Events with index exactly equal to the clock tick are **included** in that bar
  (the interval is closed on the right: `(prev_tick, tick]`).
- Inside a `Pipeline` this holds when a node releases values late, such as a
  `Filter`, a `threshold=` or `count=` `Resample`, or a `CombineLatest` upstream:
  a tick emits its bar once no value at or below it can still come. Clock events
  at one index give one bar.
- In a live session (`pipe.live()`), the bar of tick `t` comes out once the
  value stream has passed `t`: a value event above `t`, an `advance(now)` with
  `now > t`, or `flush()`. A value at `t` still joins the bar, so `advance(t)`
  is not enough. After `push("v", 50, ...)`, `push("c", 60, ...)` and
  `push("c", 70, ...)`, bar 60 comes out at `advance(61)`, not at
  `advance(60)`. 2.8.0 emitted it at the next event of either input (here the
  tick at 70), which put a later value into an earlier bar when the inputs
  came in a different order. A batch or lazy call gives the same bars.
- There is no trailing partial bucket: only explicit clock ticks trigger emission.
- Works in eager, `Pipeline` graph, and lazy iterator regimes with identical results.

**Graph regime.** Wire two `Input` nodes and pass `clock=True`:
`x = Input('price'); clk = Input('obs'); node = Resample(x, clk, clock=True, agg='last', fill='carry');
dag = Pipeline([x, clk], [node])`.

Select.name: Select
Select.title: Select
Select.short: Pick column(s) from a wide (M, N) value stream.
Select.details:
Pick one or more columns from a wide `(rows, columns)` value stream by position.
The index and the number of rows are unchanged; only the width changes. Usable
eagerly and inside a `Pipeline`.

Feeding a lazy iterator of `(value, index)` pairs returns a lazy iterator of column-selected events; feeding arrays or `(values, index)` tuples returns the batch result.

stream-tuple-convention.name: stream-tuple-convention
stream-tuple-convention.title: Stream tuple convention
stream-tuple-convention.short: The (values, index) tuple at every operator boundary.
stream-tuple-convention.details:
Every screamer stream operator accepts and returns plain `(values, index)`
2-tuples at the batch boundary.

- **`values`** - a 1-D `(T,)` or 2-D `(T, N)` NumPy array.
- **`index`** - a 1-D array of length `T`, or `None` for positional streams
  (row number as ordering coordinate).

from_pandas.name: from_pandas
from_pandas.title: from_pandas
from_pandas.short: Convert a pandas Series or DataFrame to a (values, index) tuple.
from_pandas.details:
Free helper: converts a pandas Series or DataFrame to the screamer
`(values, index)` tuple convention. The pandas data becomes the values array
and the pandas index becomes the index array.

reshape.name: reshape
reshape.title: reshape
reshape.short: Name the axes of data with a layout string (T, A, F) and reshape it to match.
reshape.details:
Free helper: names the axes of data with a layout string and reshapes it to
match. A **layout** spells out the axes of the input in order with the letters
`T` (time), `A` (asset), and `F` (field): `"TA"` reads a `(T, K)` array as `K`
assets, and `"TF"` reads it as one series with `K` fields. Without `->` the
result is the canonical `(T, *A, F)` shape that every screamer function reads;
an optional `->` names the wanted result instead.

split.name: split
split.title: split
split.short: Partition a merged tagged stream back into per-source streams.
split.details:
The inverse of `Merge`: partition a source-tagged stream back into one stream per
source. `split(*Merge()(a_v, b_v, index=[a_k, b_k]))` reconstructs the original
streams.

Event `i` goes to output `sources[i]`, in event order. `values` may have any
rank with time first, `(T, ...)`: each event is a row, and each output keeps the
row shape, `(rows, ...)`. A source is a whole number: a bool, a fractional or a
non-finite source raises `TypeError`. It is from 0 to 2147483646, one less than
the most outputs (2**31 - 1); another source raises `ValueError`. `n` sets the
number of outputs, by default `max(sources) + 1`; an `n` at or below the largest
source raises `ValueError`, since events would be dropped. A split makes at most
2\*\*20 (1048576) outputs: more, from a large source or `n`, raises `ValueError`
before anything is allocated.

to_pandas.name: to_pandas
to_pandas.title: to_pandas
to_pandas.short: Convert a (values, index) tuple to a pandas Series or DataFrame.
to_pandas.details:
Free helper: converts the screamer `(values, index)` tuple convention to a
pandas Series (1-D) or DataFrame (2-D). Pass `columns` to label a 2-D result.
A positional stream (`index=None`) gets pandas' default RangeIndex.

forecast_pairs.name: forecast_pairs
forecast_pairs.title: forecast_pairs
forecast_pairs.short: Build a forecasting training set where row t holds the features at t and the target over the horizon after t.
forecast_pairs.details:
`forecast_pairs(X, y, count=h)` is a helper that builds a training set: row `t`
holds the features `X[t]` and the target over the next `h` events. With
`duration=` the horizon is a span of the index instead of a number of events.
The target `y` is a causal series, so its value at step `t` is known at `t`: a
target over a horizon is stamped at the end of that horizon. For example
`LogReturn(h)(price)` at step `t` is the return over `(t - h, t]`, and
`forecast_pairs` moves it back to the row of the features it follows.

A training row and a live row differ only in the target:

| | features | target |
|---|---|---|
| training, row t | `X[t]` | outcome of `(t, t + h]` |
| live, row t | `X[t]` | NaN, not known yet |

The [labels guide](../labels.md) shows how a target is built for each kind of
prediction.

`index` chooses whose timestamp a row carries:

| | row holds | NaN padding |
|---|---|---|
| `index="features"` (default) | `X[t]` and the target over `(t, t + h]` | the last `h` targets |
| `index="target"` | `X[t - h]` and `y[t]` | the first `h` feature rows |

In count mode both settings hold the same pairs and differ only in the stamp
and in where the padding is. With `dropna=True` they return identical arrays.
